paragraphs.text: "The words of the Preacher (Qoheleth), the son of David, king in Jerusalem [1].

He is Solomon. Although he did not identify himself by name, he is the son of David, the king in Jerusalem, who, because of his wealth, his wisdom and his worldwide concern in that day, had a great opportunity to test temporal life and to offer this experience to all mankind. We note here:

a. He concealed his name "Solomon," which means "peace," because sin had shattered his inner peace and brought troubles upon himself and upon his kingdom, just as it shattered his peace with God, so that he no longer deserved this name. It is as though he were saying, "Do not call me a man of peace, but call me bitter" (Ruth 1:20).

b. He called himself "the Preacher" (the Gatherer), because God had gathered him through repentance into His holy flock after he had strayed like a lost sheep; now He brings him back from his wandering to the holy Church through reconciliation with God. Or because he offers his experience and practical wisdom to mankind, so that all may return to the catholic Church. As for his use of the feminine form [the Preacher], perhaps it was a rebuke to himself, since he clung to foreign women and because of them turned aside to idol worship.

c. He mentions David's fatherhood to him in order to rebuke himself: that he, the son of that great saint, the author of the Psalms, had wandered and gone astray. And perhaps also to stir hope within himself, for his father David had fallen and risen again, and by his rising from sin he urged many to repentance.
d. "King in Jerusalem": he sinned against God, who made him king and did not let him lack anything. What multiplies his sin is that he reigned over the holy city of God, Jerusalem.
"Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher:
Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" [2-3].

The word "vanity" in Hebrew, hebel, basically means "breath" (Isa 57:13) or "vapor," as though the whole world apart from God were like a breath that goes out of a man's nose or a vapor that comes from his mouth on a cold day; he can no longer hold it or be occupied with it, because it quickly disperses into the air.

By the word vanity he means that the world is temporal and passing, and that it is without profit in the long run of eternity. Here it is not a solitary monk who offers us his experience and thoughts, but a rich and influential king, with experience in every aspect of life of that time... a realistic and practical discourse.
The author affirmed in more than one place that everything in the world is good and useful as a gift of God, but man's misuse of it made it vain, since "the mind itself became vain" (Eph 4:17).

He does not push us toward a spirit of despair, but demands of us that our thoughts not be absorbed in earthly and temporal things, and that they not become a goal for us in our worship. In other words, life in all its aspects has no meaning and no benefit, being shallow and passing, unless it is truly bound to God; then, and only then, when it rests on God and on His word, does it have value.
* Why are you bound by the love of temporary things?

Why do you run after the things that hold the last place, as though they had the first priority, though they are vain and a lie? For you want them to dwell with you, while they pass away like a shadow.
St. Augustine * Calls everything we see and struggle for, as a visible reality, "vanity."
What is vain lacks "substance," and what lacks "substance" carries no power!

St. Gregory of Nyssa * "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Let us go to the tombs; show me your father, show me your wife. Where is the one who wore gilded garments? The one who rode in the chariot? The one who had armies, who had a girdle of office, and who had heralds? The one who killed these and cast those into prison? Who put to death whom he would and pardoned whom he would? I see nothing but bones, worms and spiders' webs. All these are dust, weakness, a dream, a shadow, a mere (frail) relation and an image, indeed not even reaching the level of an image.

St. John Chrysostom The aim of affirming the vanity of this world is to train the heart not to hate the world but rather to love heaven and to enjoy God the Word, as the Eternal One who satisfies the soul:

* "All is vanity, saith the Preacher," everything in this world. Therefore whoever desires salvation, let him rise above the world and seek the "Word" who is with God, fleeing from this world and leaving the earth. For no one can grasp what exists always unless he first flees from here. For this reason also, when the Lord wished to draw near to God the Father (who is one with Him), He said to His disciples, "Arise, let us go hence" (Jn 14:31).
St. Ambrose * [In the words of the Lord Christ, the Word of God who satisfies the soul]
I am your father, your brother, your bridegroom, your house, your garment, your source and your foundation.
I am everything you long for; so you will lack nothing.
I will be your servant, for I came to serve, not to be served.
I am your friend, your member, your head, your brother, your sister, your mother, and everything to you... only be a friend to me...
What more do you seek?
Why do you turn away the One who loves you?
Why do you toil for this world?
Why do you draw water with a leaking vessel, for such is toil for the present life?
Why do you spin wool in the fire?
Why do you wrestle with the air?
Why do you run in vain?
Does not every art have a purpose? This is plain to all; but you are without aim. Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.

* Let us believe Him and hold fast to the things in which there is nothing vain, but only what is true; what is founded on solid rock, where there is no old age and no decline, but everything is flourishing and fresh, without corruption, aging or dissolution.
I ask you that we love God with a sincere affection, not for fear of hell, but out of desire for the Kingdom.
What can be compared to seeing Christ? Certainly nothing!

What delight shall we obtain from these good things...? "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1 Cor 2:9).
St. John Chrysostom * It is not one who has become a companion of the angels and has grown familiar with their mysteries and has not despised the company of the world.
* If you leave your possessions for His sake, you will possess Him in yourself forever.

How sweet is the departure of those who love You to You, O Physician, and how hard is the departure of the lovers of the world from it, because those move on to their inheritance, while these depart from what is theirs.
* Who is this who has tasted the sweetness of the fruits of the tree of life and wants to run after the foul fruits of the world?!
St. John Saba The question that many have raised: Why is the world called vain when it was made by God, who is all good? In other words: does the good God create something without benefit?

God sees that everything He created is "good" (Gen 1:10, 12, 18, 31); but man, whose mind, nature and inner insight were corrupted, wronged his view of the world as he wronged his use of it, so the world became vain. The world, which is God's handiwork, is good; it was created for man, that he might work in it and rejoice... But now that man has been shattered in his nature, the world no longer fulfills its purpose as his servant.

* If (creation) is the works of God, how can it be vain? The dispute over this matter is great. But hear, beloved: it is not the works of God that we call vain, God forbid! The heaven is not vain; the earth is not vain, God forbid! Neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars, nor our bodies. No! For all these are very good (Gen 1:31).

What, then, is the vain thing? Let us hear the Preacher himself, when he says, "I planted vineyards for myself; I got me men singers and women singers; I made me pools of water; and I had possessions of herds and flocks; I gathered me also silver and gold; and I saw that all these were vanity" (cf. Eccl 2:4-8). And he says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" (Eccl 12:8). Hear also what the prophet says: "He heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them" (Ps 39:6). Such is vain: your magnificent buildings, your excessive wealth, the crowd of slaves jostling in the public square, your vain glory and pomp, your haughty thoughts and your boasting; all these are vain, for they are not from the hand of God but are from your own doing. And why are they vain? Because they have no useful end.

St. John Chrysostom St. John Chrysostom speaks to us, in his treatise "No one can harm a man unless he harms himself," about the concept of goodness at some length, explaining that the world with all that is in it is neither good nor evil in itself, but man's use of it turns it to good or to evil. Whoever uses money for evil, it becomes evil to him; and whoever supports his needy brethren with it, it becomes a blessing to him, and so on...

Finally, St. Augustine sees that it befits the believer to transfer his temporal possessions to the true life through almsgiving, saying: [We must hold fast to the true life, so let us transfer our wealth to the place of the true life, and there we shall find what we gave here. He (God) accomplishes this transfer of our possessions, He who wrought the change in our souls]. The Lord Christ, who has seated us in the heavenlies, transfers our money to heaven!

Although man, by the corruption of his nature, mind and inner insight, has made the world vain, man remains in God's eyes more precious than the whole world! "What is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mt 16:26). For God created the world for man, not man for the world. Therefore it befits man in his striving and labor, whether in his private life, his family life, his work or his worship, not to turn his gaze away from his inner life and its satisfaction in God Himself. For this reason the Preacher warns us against every striving in which man loses his goal, saying, "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?!" [3]. Our labor in our daily life and in our worship will not be able to satisfy the soul, atone for its sin, heal its wounds and sanctify it, unless we lean on the Savior's breast by practical faith and ask for the work of His Holy Spirit in us.
* Man's righteousness is counted as nothing. The work of men, what is it? All their labor is vain.
From You, O Lord, and by Your grace our nature becomes good. From You is righteousness; so we men become righteous. From You are mercy and grace. So we are changed from dust into Your image.
Give strength to our will, so that we may not sink into sin.

St. Ephrem the Syrian As long as we are "under the sun," we are subject to trials and suffer from its heat (Mt 20:12). And we shall gain nothing from all our labor; but if we receive the Sun of Righteousness within us, He lifts us above every evil trial, and the flame of passions cannot touch our inner depths. The Sun of Righteousness bears us up by His Holy Spirit so that the soul may enjoy the pledge of eternal glory, and we say, "He made us sit together with Him in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6).

* By "labor" here [3] he points to the life of the flesh, which seeks no profit in any good work. It says, "What profit hath a man?", that is, what does the soul gather from all the labor of life, in the life of those who live only for luxuries.
St. Gregory of Nyssa

4 One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever. 5 The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. 6 The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. 7 All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. 8 All speech falls short. Man cannot declare it all. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. 9 The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun. 10 If anything is found of which it is said, "See, this is new!" it was already of old time, in the ages which were before us. 11 There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after.

The Preacher offers real examples from nature that confirm the brevity of temporal life, its changing nature and its inability to satisfy the heart; that there is truly nothing new in life despite progress and development; and finally, that whatever honor or desire man attains, time wipes out by forgetfulness.

entries.section: a. The brevity of human life:

paragraphs.text: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever" [4].

The Preacher shows that the period of our enjoyment of earthly things is extremely short. For although the earth was created for man and for his comfort, man lives in a generation that ends with him, to be replaced by another generation, while the earth remains until the end of the age.

* The mortal remains mortal, whether honored or not honored... The wise Preacher says, "The earth abideth for ever," serving every generation, the first and the next that is born after it upon it; but men... come into life by the will of their Creator without knowing it, and are taken from it before they wish it. And yet, in spite of this extreme vanity, they think they are the masters of the earth.
St. Gregory of Nyssa

entries.section: b. The changing nature of all beings:

paragraphs.text: Everything in the world changes; the sun rises and sets, then returns and rises... and so the movement never stops. The position of the earth in relation to the sun changes, so that sunrise and sunset occur, which is repeated daily.
So also the winds move in certain courses; and the waters also move, as they evaporate and become clouds, then rain, then rivers, and return to the seas and oceans to evaporate again!

Our looking at nature and the changes it contains, which touch all beings, reveals to us the nature of the world, that it is not stable but ever changing, and therefore will not remain forever. It is as though it does not befit man, who carries within him a natural longing for immortality, to attach himself to what is changing and passing away.
And perhaps the author wanted to show that man, for whose sake nature moves before him, the beings such as the stars, the winds and the clouds, is himself helpless; what is in his hand?!

And perhaps he also wanted to declare that nature itself changes, the sunrise being followed by sunset and then sunrise again, and so on... while man is unable to move; he is born, then dies and does not rise again upon the same earth! How great is man, for whose sake this universe exists with all its known and hidden powers and laws, and how weak he is, for it is hard for him to change even his inner nature?! Man is great in God, who gives him everything, and exceedingly weak in himself alone!

* We see in the sun a symbol of the rising and setting of our nature. There is one road for all, there is one circle for everyone in the journey of life. By birth we rise, then we descend again to our natural place. And when we reach the sunset of life, our light sinks down below the earth... What is of the earth dissolves completely into its element, and the circle continues on its way again and again.
St. Gregory of Nyssa
"All speech falls short.
Man cannot declare it all.
The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing" [8].

Can we expect satisfaction for a soul made in the image of God from temporal, passing things full of toil?! For nature, with all its resources, cannot satisfy even the senses of sight, hearing or smell, so how can it satisfy the inner life?!
* We wake every day to eat and drink, and yet no one is satisfied so as not to hunger or thirst again shortly.
We seek gain every day, and greed has no limits!
"The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing." He that loveth silver is not satisfied with silver.
There is no limit to toil, and no profit in wealth.
St. Ambrose

entries.section: d. There is nothing new in creation:

paragraphs.text: With all the wealth, increasing pleasures, fame and glory that the Preacher obtained, he realized that there is nothing new under the sun. True, outward circumstances and man's capabilities develop, but his nature, and also his feelings and motives, remain as they have been since the first man was created. What aroused the instinct of the young man in the last century may be loathed by the young man of today, but the nature of the instincts in a young man's life remains the same through the ages, even if the form of the stimulus differs. Everything under the sun has not changed; what is new is what is above the sun, that is, the enjoyment of the new life we have in Christ Jesus, the Sun of Righteousness, and we hear Him say, "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). We say with the Apostle Paul: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new" (2 Cor 5:17).

Man often feels the need for renewal... He seeks what is new merely because it is new, and rejects what is old merely because it is old. This feeling springs from an inner need that touches the very being of his nature, but instead of renewing his nature by the Spirit of God, he seeks an outward renewal or change, such as new models, new theories and new expressions. So you find modern man wanting, if possible, to renew everything around him, not only his work, his house, his city or his car, but sometimes his husband or wife... He feels a measure of boredom and seeks renewal!

The soul that is united to the Lord Christ as its Bridegroom is led by the Holy Spirit to continual renewal in inward thought, so it feels no boredom or weariness, but lives rejoicing in the Spirit as in heaven, untouched by old age and unaffected by aging.

* Because God is perfect, He became perfect man, and entered with all that is new into perfection; this is the only new thing under the sun, through which He declared the riches of God's surpassing power!
Fr. John of Damascus

entries.section: e. Forgetfulness is the mark of every age:

paragraphs.text: "There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after" [11].

Man lives longing to immortalize his memory or the memory of his family, but the world forgets the former ones, and we who are the latter will be forgotten by the coming generations. What, then, is the profit to man if he concentrates his labor on acquiring the wealth or glory of the world? Wealth passes away, and glory is forgotten! Even mere remembrance, time is able to destroy.

12 I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem. 13 And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith. 14 I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. 15 That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. 16 I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge. 17 And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit. 18 For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.

The Preacher presented proofs from the reality of nature concerning the vanity of the world: its passing away, its instability, and its inability to satisfy the inner man or to renew corrupt human nature, showing that time takes from man even the fame or glory for which he spared no effort. Now, being a great king who lacks nothing, he pursues human wisdom, examining by wisdom what goes on in the world so as to have knowledge and learning... and behold, he arrives at a negative experience that does not satisfy.
a. "I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven" [12-13].

He set his heart to seek and search out by wisdom, instead of lifting his heart to God to ask for heavenly wisdom (Jas 1:5). He needed to enter into dialogue with God, who alone gives constructive heavenly wisdom, instead of dialogue with himself outside the circle of God, to obtain human wisdom that is unable to satisfy his soul... "For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow" [18].

The wisdom of God reveals our weaknesses, but it gives us hope and offers us possibilities for work; whereas human wisdom, though it shows the weaknesses, leads us into grief and despair: Who will renew my nature, whose corruption I have discovered? Who can set right my inner and outer circumstances? Who will move the world for my edification? The Preacher says, "That which is crooked cannot be made straight, and that which is wanting cannot be numbered" [15]... a bitter feeling of complete inability to set things right.

* The stubborn man cannot become virtuous (by his wisdom), nor the corrupt man become respected... We can also understand this verse [15] thus: there is such great evil in this world that it is hard to return to the original state of right order. It is not easy to return to what (man) was in his first creation, in perfection and order; but through repentance everything can be restored to uprightness, though Satan remains resistant in his error.

St. Jerome Here it befits us to distinguish between recourse to human wisdom alone, relying on bare human experience, and the sanctification of human thought and human experience by the work of God. For this reason we are not surprised to see St. Clement of Alexandria believe that there is no enmity between faith and philosophy; the latter is not a work of darkness as some suppose, but carries a partial truth, which needs perfecting and purifying from all the impurities that entered into it, through the work of faith. As for the Fathers who attacked human wisdom, they attacked only reliance on it outside the circle of God.

* In my opinion every sensible man thinks that learning is the chief of all that is good... We must keep what can help us to contemplate the truth, avoiding everything that leads to evil, error and destruction.
* It is necessary to use discernment in education, in such a way that we choose useful learning and avoid everything harmful and ominous.

* We must begin by reading worldly thought in order to rise afterward to the holy things and the mysteries of the faith... If there is agreement between this culture and our doctrines, knowing it is of great benefit; and if not, the comparison in the opposite case will confirm our correct beliefs.

St. Basil the Great Let us seek the wisdom that is mixed with humility and agrees with the spirit of faith; but the wisdom that springs from man's pride, his self-reliance and his separation from his Creator is a hindrance... The Fathers call it "the wisdom of this world."
* No one is wise in knowledge except the one who has put away from himself the wisdom of this world.
* Despise your wisdom and reject it, that the wisdom of the Lord may dwell in you.

St. John Saba b. If God gave man a longing to seek wisdom and to search into all things, this wisdom revealed to the Preacher that the life God gave him is a sore travail [13]; for many ask: Why did God place us in a world full of misery?
God did not create us to live in a world of misery and toil, but the misuse of the world and the wrong view of it corrupted our life and distorted the image of the world in our eyes.
"I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation (a seizing) of spirit" [14].

What does "vexation of spirit" (a seizing of the wind) mean? Some translate it "wrestling with the wind" or "feeding on the wind," that is, that feeding on food is of no value, like the wind; or that the soul in its hunger grasps everything around it in the world to eat it, and behold, it eats wind. This points to the loss of purpose in human activities, their barrenness, and their inability to give true satisfaction within man, or inner reform and healing. St. Augustine sees that the seizing of the wind points to the vain pride into which man falls by seeking temporary things.

This is what the Preacher reached through the wisdom and knowledge he received as king of Israel, and the neighboring peoples were accustomed to say, "This great nation is a wise and understanding people" (Deut 4:6). And Solomon was known for wisdom, as he says: "I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge" [16].

c. The Preacher offers us his experience as he pursues wisdom, learning and knowledge, the greatest things in the world, "for in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow" [18]. Here he does not attack wisdom or learning, but declares their inability to bring happiness and joy to man. For by wisdom and learning, as we said before, man discovers his need of many things he cannot attain, and so he is filled with sorrow. As St. Augustine says: [Whenever I long for much and do not find it here, does not my sorrow for it increase the more until it is fulfilled? Do I not weep the more until what I seek is accomplished?!]. He also says: [By obtaining this knowledge he gains sorrow also, because of his inability to fulfil the desire to reach his fitting homeland, his Creator and his blessed God]. And St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [Solomon says: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me. Truly he who increases in knowledge increases in grief. For the joy that springs from what we discover is not greater than the pain because of what (we do not obtain but) escapes us; it is a pain that I imagine like that felt by those who are drawn up from the waters while thirsty, or those who are unable to reach what they think they are holding, or one who is suddenly left in darkness by the burst of a swift flash of light].

This is the work of wisdom, the greatest thing we possess here; what, then, are the rest of the things of the world? We need the "wisdom of God," who alone is able to satisfy the soul, not temporal, earthly wisdom.

"Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory" (1 Cor 2:6-7).
"But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 1:30).
Therefore let us possess our Christ within us; He is the true wisdom, and He alone is able to save our souls, satisfy them, make them grow and glorify them!

1 I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity. 2 I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it? 3 I thought in mine heart to cheer my body with wine, my heart meditating on wisdom, and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life.

The Preacher (Qoheleth) tried to find what he sought in frenzied pleasure or sensual excitement, so he turned to bodily delights as a source that might give him satisfaction; he went on drawing from the sensual pleasures of food, which are symbolized by wine, and they gave him a passing, temporary pleasure, not lasting satisfaction.
"I said in mine heart,
Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure (enjoy happiness).
And, behold, this also is vanity.
I said of laughter, It is mad!
And of mirth, What doeth it?!" [1-2].

Solomon communed with his heart instead of discussing the matter with God in a spirit of prayer and godliness, saying: Try laughter, eating and drinking (wine), drive away care and enjoy happiness; just as the rich fool said, "And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Lk 12:19).

Many think that happiness lies in a life of amusement, parties and temporal joys, with the eating, drinking, entertainment and laughter they contain... These do not distinguish between inner joy, which gives constant cheerfulness and true peace, and the laughter of amusement, which springs from an inner emptiness. Inner joy is food for the soul; it nourishes it and makes it grow, so that it widens to carry within it the joyful Kingdom of God. But temporal joy outside the circle of God numbs man and does not satisfy his depths, but rather increases his sorrow... Therefore the wise man calls it mad! Many resort to drugs and bad companions to escape their problems, and behold, they throw themselves into graver problems that touch their inner being.

He said of laughter, "It is mad," because it cannot turn the heart to true happiness, but only offers a temporary covering for inner sorrow and hidden bitterness. And perhaps he calls it so because it urges him to go far from God, who is "the true joy," for it is said: "They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave. Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways" (Job 21:12-14).

He says to outward joy, What doeth it? For he realizes that laughter does not reform the heart and does not remove its gloom. Therefore it is said: "He that singeth songs to a heavy (troubled) heart" (Prov 25:20)... Instead of amusement it would have befitted him to resort to the tears of repentance, which give inner joy and sincere cheerfulness, because sin breaks the heart and fills it with bitter gloom!

Along with laughter or amusement, Solomon resorted to drinking wine, thinking that he was able to cheer his body with wine while his heart meditated on wisdom [3]; that is, he drank it in order to gain experience and to see whether wine could satisfy his life, but he found folly in it, because "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and whosoever reeleth thereby is not wise" (Prov 20:1). In this he is like one who wanted to serve God and mammon at the same time.

St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the danger of pursuing pleasures, saying: [Animals are earthly and incline toward the earth... their heads are bowed toward the ground, and they look to their bellies, searching for the things that please them. But you, O man, your head is lifted toward heaven, and your eyes look upward; so if you are defiled with the lusts of the flesh, and are enslaved to the pleasures of the belly and the lower pleasures, you thereby draw near to the unreasoning animals and become like them. I propose to you to care for another matter that befits you: "Seek those things which are above, where Christ is" (Col 3:1). Rise above the passing things of the world, and learn from your bodily constitution, and make it a rule for your life. Your city is heaven, and your true homeland is the Jerusalem above, and your fellow citizens are the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven].

Again he says: [Philosophers and thinkers were eager to search for the end of man on this earth. But they differed among themselves in this matter, their opinions conflicted and their schools multiplied. Some of them claimed that the end of man is knowledge, while others said it is work. Some said that the end of man is to despise the body and subject it to the control of the mind, and to strengthen the spirit and regard it as the greatest power in man, while others said that the end of man in this life is only the enjoyment of pleasures and the good things of life. As for us, the end we seek and aspire to reach with all care and diligence is the blessed life with God in the everlasting heaven, and nothing in the world equals this praiseworthy pursuit in honor and greatness for the rational creature].

4 I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: 5 I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: 6 I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees: 7 I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me: 8 I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, a lady and ladies. 9 So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me. 10 And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. 11 Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.

The Preacher furnished himself with worldly delights, magnificent buildings, slaves, silver and gold, and the things that belong to kings alone; yet this was not from a regression to, or an escape into, uncommitted childhood, as the Greeks did, immersed in pleasures and occupied with appearances to escape responsibility. As it is written in the Book of Wisdom: "For they said within themselves, reasoning not aright, Our life is short and sorrowful... Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and use pleasures in the wilderness while it is the time of old age, and let us fill ourselves with excellent wine and perfumes, and let no breeze of the flowers of spring pass us by..." (Wis 2:1, 6, 7).
Rather, it was the custom of the Jews to express power by holding feasts and building magnificent buildings, and in short, by becoming a master of the arts.

a. He was deeply absorbed in construction and building, in cities as in villages, for he says: "I builded me houses" [4]. It was said of him: "And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer... And all the cities of store that Solomon had, and cities for his chariots, and cities for his horsemen, and that which Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion" (1 Kgs 9:15-19). He built many buildings, but he began by building the house of the Lord, not like those to whom it was said: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" (Hag 1:3)... He also employed many poor workers for their benefit. This is the good side of Solomon in his concern for construction and building; but perhaps what spoiled his work for a time was his thinking that these projects could satisfy his soul and quench his desire for temporal glory, for he says: "I made me great works" [4].

Building houses is not a sin, but the sin is to be occupied with building houses for the comfort of our bodies without offering a house to the Lord in our depths. Let the Lord rest in our hearts, and He will give rest to our bodies also, and will kindle our hearts with the fire of love, so that we long to depart and dwell with Him and rest in His divine embrace, instead of being occupied with temporal greatness and vain glory. Let the Lord dwell in our hearts as His own house, and let us dwell in His heavens as our own eternal home, and the whole world will not be able to draw us to itself.
* He who flees from vain glory with understanding tastes in himself (the hope of) the age to come.

* As soon as a man chooses to be free from possessions, his mind is occupied with departing from the world; he makes the life after the resurrection his constant meditation, and strives toward constant readiness (for departure), which is profitable to him; he begins to despise everything that brings (temporal) honor or bodily comfort, and this penetrates his thoughts, and his mind is always refreshed by thinking of despising the world.
St. Isaac the Syrian The Fathers urge us to build the inner house of the Lord, His temple and His altar, in our hearts:
* Make me worthy, my Lord Jesus Christ, to take part in building Your house...!
But the dwelling of the Lord that He wants us to build is holiness... By this every man can set up a tabernacle for God within his heart.

* Let the soul have an altar in the midst of the heart, on which the sacrifices of prayer and the burnt offerings of mercy are offered, and upon it the bulls of pride are slaughtered with the knife of meekness, and the rams of anger and the goats of luxury and lusts are killed...
Let the soul know how to set up, within the holy of holies of its heart, a lampstand that shines without ceasing!
Origen b. He cared for planting gardens: "I planted vineyards for myself; I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits" [4-5].

God gave the first man the garden of Eden to work in, containing trees of every fruit, and also including the tree of life... So God wants to satisfy the body with every temporal fruit and to satisfy the soul with the tree of immortal life, but man cared for what satisfies his body and not his soul. Therefore the Lord Christ came to our earth, and His body was hung on the tree, that we may stretch out our hands and pluck from it the fruit of life. Let the Cross be planted in our souls and let us gather the fruit of the Holy Spirit in us, so that our view of every fruit may be sanctified, and man may be satisfied in body and spirit.
Our Christ plants His Cross in our hearts and sets up from it a joyful paradise, bearing the fruit of the Holy Spirit that gladdens heavenly and earthly beings!
c. He made many channels for watering: "I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees" [6].
We need the fountain of living water, that is, the Holy Spirit of God, who waters our inner wilderness and sets up from it a holy garden.
d. He got servants and maidens who bore him servants born in the house for his service [7].

e. He got cattle, silver, gold and the peculiar treasure of kings [7-8]. He became extremely rich, for it was said of him: "And the king made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance" (1 Kgs 10:27).
What does "the peculiar treasure of kings" mean? What belongs to kings, or what kings alone, among all the nobles and great men, have of possessions or particular property.

The expression "peculiar treasure" in Hebrew, s’qulia, basically means "property," but it came to be used generally for property of high value. The people of God were called "a people of possession" (Ex 19:5), as a people whom God chose to be His portion, and who are exceedingly precious in His eyes.

Solomon acquired what belongs to kings as a precious thing... But to you the King of kings Himself is offered, that you may possess Him and He may possess you; you become His portion and He is your portion, and you say, "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine." This is what satisfies your inner depths, which God created in His image, and no one else can satisfy them!

The Preacher has shown in more than one place that wealth and possessions are not an evil thing; rather, the evil lies in the corruption of our will and our wrong view of them, and also in the deviation of our aim:
* Be watchful in using your riches, lest God's gift to you remain useless in your hands.
Do you have gold and silver? If you handle them well, they will be good for you. And if you are wicked, you will misuse them.
Gold and silver are evil to the wicked and good to the righteous, not because gold and silver make men righteous, but because righteous men use them for good...
What use is what you have in your possession, when you do not possess the One who gave you everything?!...
Do you want to keep your wealth? Manage it as you wish; if you find a better guardian for it than Christ, hand it over to him...
Christ is with you to take your money and keep it for you; He will not betray you, but will carry your treasure faithfully.
St. Augustine In the second century St. Clement of Alexandria wrote a book entitled "Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?" in which he explains the Christian view of wealth; in it he says:
[We do not cast the rich man to the ground, he who benefits our brethren...

Man does not squander his wealth; rather it befits him to destroy his inner lusts that conflict with the good use of wealth. For when a man becomes virtuous and good, he can use this wealth in a good way.
So let us understand the leaving of our possessions (Mk 10:17-31) and the selling of them as a leaving and selling of the lusts of our souls].

f. He provided for himself, to no avail, every licentious atmosphere of male singers and female singers, a lady and ladies [8]... He did not deprive his body or his heart of material or immaterial pleasures.

With the riches and pleasures he enjoyed, he gained temporal glory and his human wisdom remained with him, for he says: "So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me" [9].

But the experience he gained from all this is: "Whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy... Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun" [10-11].

God wants our rest and our joy, but our preoccupation with the pleasures and wealth of the world often draws our heart away from the rest that is in Christ Jesus, and from the enjoyment of fellowship in the heavenly glories.
* The mind of the man who flees from the comfort of this age gazes intently at the age to come. He who is captive to possessions is their slave.

* Blessed is the man who stops his ears to all the delights that separate him from his Creator, for he eats only one delicious food from the table of the Most High, the food on which the heavenly powers feed.
Blessed is he who takes as his food the living Bread that came down from heaven, that Bread that gives light to the world, that supports the ages of the new world.

Blessed is he who sees in his drink the watered spring of life, flowing from the bosom of the Father in His mercy; for when he drinks from it his eyes are fixed on Him, his heart rejoices and flourishes anew, and is filled with joy and gladness. He who beholds his Lord in his food is content with Him and enjoys fellowship with Him alone, and has no fellowship with the unworthy lest he be deprived of His splendor...
The man who has friends for the purpose of filling his belly is like a wolf feeding on carrion!
How terrible is your greed, you fool, for you want to fill your belly with every lust!
These warnings are sufficient for those who are able to control their bellies.
* He who is occupied with many concerns is a slave to many, but he who abandons them all and cares only for himself is a friend of God!
* Lord, count me worthy to hate my (temporal) life for the sake of the life that is in You!

St. Isaac the Syrian The Fathers of the Church give us their spiritual experience regarding the enjoyment of bodily pleasures, summed up in the necessity of keeping to the middle or moderate way, which they call the royal way.
* Do not fill your belly too much, lest fornication torment you, and do not weaken your body, lest those who hate you rejoice over you.
Hold to a moderate rank, and behold, you are walking the royal way, and your journey will be without fear.
St. John Saba The Preacher sums up his experience with worldly pleasures, saying: "Behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun" [11].

* The Preacher says, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." But if all creation is good as the work of the hands of the good Creator, how can everything be vain? If the earth is vain, are the heavens also vain...? And also the angels, thrones, dominions, powers and the rest of the orders? Never! If things that are good in themselves, as the creation of the good Creator, have been called vain, it is only by comparison with what is higher and greater than they. For example, if a lamp is compared with a lantern, it is counted less than it; and if the lantern is compared with a star, it gives no light at all. And if a star shines, it grows pale before the moon, and the moon appears dim before the sun, and if the sun is compared with Christ, it is counted darkness. So God says, "I AM THAT I AM"; when all creatures are compared with Him, they are counted as non-existent.

St. Jerome The author concludes his discourse on sensual pleasures by saying: "And there was no profit under the sun" [11]. It is as though he were saying: Who will carry me to what is above the sun? Who will lift me above time? I need the Lord Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, and the wisdom of God.
Thus he moves from the unsatisfying sensual pleasures to speak of temporal wisdom, which, though better than ignorance or folly, cannot satisfy the soul as the wisdom of God does!

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: 12 And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what is the man who cometh after the king, whom they appointed long ago? 13 Then I saw that wisdom hath more profit than folly, as light hath more profit than darkness. 14 The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all. 15 Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity. 16 For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that as of old, so the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool. 17 Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit. 18 Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. 19 And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity.
The author draws a comparison between wisdom and folly, presenting the following experience:

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: a. "I saw that wisdom hath more profit than folly, as light hath more profit than darkness" [13]. The Preacher does not ignore natural wisdom or the wisdom that comes from human experience, likening wisdom to light and folly to darkness. Wisdom is useful but does not satisfy; but the Lord Christ, who is the heavenly wisdom of God, is both useful and satisfying; He is the light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world, dispelling the darkness of our corruption and offering Himself to us as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

St. John Chrysostom sees that wisdom is useful even for the poor man, because it gives him light so that he does not live in darkness, whereas ignorance destroys the rich man, who in his greed and love of money lives in a darkness that does not let him see things as he ought. One who stands in a dark place does not see what is around him, even if it is a vessel of gold or a precious stone or costly garments... he counts them all as nothing, does not appreciate their value and does not see their beauty; so the greedy man does not perceive the value of the things worthy of our concern.

Let us enjoy the Lord Christ, the true "Wisdom," and be enlightened by His Holy Spirit, the giver of love, joy and peace... And let us leave folly, lest we care for dust and do not care for heaven! Folly is a darkness that corrupts our view of God and His Kingdom, and even of ourselves and our brethren, as well as of the world and all that is in it!
* How great is the difference between wisdom and folly; they differ as day differs from night.

He who chooses virtue is like one who sees all things with perfect clarity, like one who looks upward and walks his paths in the brightness of the light. But he who, on the other hand, has plunged into evil is like a person wandering aimlessly on a moonless night, walking like a blind man, deprived of seeing things, like one who is in darkness. And when I contemplate the end of those patterns of life, I find no profit in the end. And as I accompany the fool, I receive the wages of folly, for what is the use of those thoughts, and what is the benefit of this multitude of words which the fool utters, since they are, so to speak, flowing from an overflow of folly?!

Also there is nothing in common between the wise man and the fool, neither as regards the remembrance of man nor God's recompense of them... The wise man never shares the fool's end. Therefore I hated my whole life, that which vanities consumed, and which I spent with a mind burdened with earthly cares.
St. Gregory the Wonderworker St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the importance of human wisdom, philosophy and the sciences, without exaggeration or ignoring of divine wisdom:

* In my opinion every sensible man thinks that learning is the chief of all that is good and within the reach of our minds. And I do not say that only our own learning is high and noble, because it despises outward elegance to cling to the beauty of thoughts, but also the learning from outside, which many Christians of little esteem reject and consider deceptive and a danger that draws us away from God... Therefore we must keep what can help us to contemplate the truth, avoiding everything that leads to evil, error and destruction.

* We must begin by reading worldly thought in order to rise afterward to the holy things and the mysteries of the faith... If there is agreement between this culture and our doctrines, knowing it is of great benefit; and if not, the comparison in the opposite case will confirm our correct beliefs.

* It is very important for us not to throw ourselves ignorantly into the sciences, but to know which of them is the most useful... and, for fear that we may cling to them and forget the knowledge of God, immersed in vain researches, he shows the necessity of discernment in education, in such a way that we choose useful learning and avoid everything harmful and ominous.

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great b. The Preacher connects wisdom with righteousness, and folly with evil, for he says: "The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness" [14]. The spiritual man is the wise man who fixes his eyes on the Lord Christ as the head of the Church, looking to Him in all his temporal and spiritual affairs, because the eyes point to looking to temporal life (the left eye) and eternal life (the right eye). The wise spiritual man sees that the Lord Christ is the center of his present and eternal life, but the fool walks in darkness, that is, in the circle of sin outside Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.

* "The wise man's eyes are in his head"; in which head? Every man, even the dull and the foolish, has his eyes in his bodily head, but the wise man has eyes (these that I just spoke of, which have been enlightened by the Lord's commandments) in his head, that is, in Christ, because "Christ is the head of the man," as the Apostle says.
Christ is the One at work in our mind.

Origen The wise man's eyes are in his head, that is, in the heavenly Lord Christ; therefore his heart also is lifted to heaven and reaches the summit, and does not remain in the mire of this world and its dust. St. Ambrose says: [The heart is all the more above the summit, because the wise man's eyes are in his head].

St. Isaac the Syrian sees that this is realized by enjoying the wisdom stored up in the words of Holy Scripture, for as the wise man is always looking to Christ the Head, that is, to the heavenly Word, his heart is lifted to behold the heavenly things.

* When a man's thoughts are wholly immersed in the delight of pursuing the wisdom stored up in the words of Holy Scripture, by his own will, gained through enlightenment from them, he puts the world behind his back and forgets everything in it, and wipes from his soul all memories that embody the world for him. Indeed, he often begins to forget ordinary thoughts that spring from the notions of human nature, and his soul remains in a state of wonder (a divine vision, ecstasy) because of the new thoughts that stir within it, arising from the sea of the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

St. Isaac the Syrian c. As for human wisdom, it is unable to lift man to the enjoyment of eternal life, or to renew his corrupt nature; so with all its usefulness it does not differ from folly, for the following reasons:
First: temporal wisdom does not carry us to what is above time; therefore, as the fool is subject to death, so the life of the wise man ends in death.
"And I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all; then said I in my heart,
As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me.
And why was I then more wise?
Then I said in my heart,
that this also is vanity...
And how dieth the wise man? as the fool!" [14-16].

Even if temporal wisdom is useful like light, it is powerless; it cannot face death or challenge it! By human wisdom and science man has advanced and satisfied many of his needs, even though his thirst for new aspirations has increased all the more; but what science cannot do is to conquer death. In Christ Jesus alone, the wisdom of God, I am able to face death, singing:
"The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death...
Death is swallowed up in victory.
O death, where is thy sting?
O grave, where is thy victory...?
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!" (1 Cor 15:26, 54-57).

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: b. Temporal wisdom gives man temporal glory and fame that may reach the ends of the earth, so that man thinks himself immortal on earth, or that his name will not be blotted out from among the sons of men... But the days pass and the wise man is forgotten just like the fool. "For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that as of old, so the days to come shall all be forgotten" [16]. We look to past time as something that has ended, and the coming days will look to our age as an old time that has been forgotten!

He who binds himself to the wheel of time, which turns with it up and down, remains in constant change, and then his remembrance ends with time; but he who binds his life to the eternal life of Christ, his life becomes continual ascents, and he enjoys strength upon strength, and grace instead of grace, and the days increase his splendor, and his glory is manifested in the great day of the Lord, and he is never forgotten!

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: c. Perhaps the wise man does not care about his life or his remembrance, reckoning that what he gathers by his experience, skill and wisdom remains for his heirs... but he does not know what they will do with what he acquired by his striving and toil. Therefore he says: "Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity" [18-19].

The wise man does not know what his heirs will do with what he acquired, but he who is bound to heavenly wisdom bequeaths to them a blessing that is not lost. What did Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth bequeath to St. John the Baptist? Their constant holy prayers and their righteousness in the Lord... so their life was a support to him while he was in the wilderness, deprived of their visible care!

Past generations handed down to us the deposit of the living Tradition, that is, practical faith in the Holy Trinity and the experience of a sincere Gospel life, as an inheritance for us to live under all circumstances, a priceless treasure! And we also must live the same living Gospel Tradition to hand it on as an inheritance to the coming generations, a mystery of blessing for many! The Church's projects or temporal possessions may be lost, but her faith is her living capital, the practical inheritance that the generations receive as their own!

entries.section: 3. The vanity of pursuing human wisdom:

paragraphs.text: Since man does not know what will befall him in the future or what his heirs will do with his labor, he lives his days in grief and sorrows, and in the night his heart takes no rest [23]; but he who is occupied with the pearl of great price, with the Lord Christ Himself, does not fear the future as though it were unknown! The first enters unconsciously into a state of despair and says: "Therefore I hated life... Yea, I hated all my labour" [17-18]; but the second, with joyful hope, says: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

20 Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun. 21 For there is a man whose labour is in wisdom, and in knowledge, and in success; yet to a man that hath not laboured therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil. 22 For what hath man of all his labour, and of the diligence of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? 23 For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.

The wise man hates life and even hates toil [17-18], for he sees it as worthless... He toils to gather fruits that fall into the grasp of another, perhaps a fool and indifferent, or into the hand of a man who does nothing to deserve to receive that wealth...
"Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun" [20].
He who is bound to temporal wisdom suffers from despair and misery, but he who is bound to divine wisdom enjoys joyful heavenly hope.

* The good man who receives wisdom from God also enjoys heavenly joy; on the other hand, the wicked man, struck by the diseases that God allows for him, and immersed in the sickness of lust, who toils for more, is soon put to shame by the one whom God has honored... for the wicked man prefers useless gifts and pursues deceit and vanities with his wretched soul.

St. Gregory the Wonderworker The wise man is not occupied with what surrounds his self (the concerns of the body), nor with what belongs to him of health, beauty and pleasure, but cares for his very self, for it is better than everything. St. Basil the Great says: [Take heed to yourself (Deut 15:9), for it is the precious treasure and the greatest good, and it deserves your keenest care... So do not care for the body nor for what is connected with the body, such as health and beauty, pleasure and long life. Likewise do not pay great attention to wealth, glory and authority, and all that is connected with earthly life. But care for yourself above everything... adorn it with virtues, cleanse it from sin, and beautify it with the adornment of virtue, which is the most beautiful adornment].

entries.section: 5. Enjoying the pleasures of ordinary life given by God:

paragraphs.text: 24 There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God. 25 For who eateth, and who enjoyeth, more than I? 26 For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit.

Lest it be thought that the author pushes us toward despair or distorts the image of the world and the body, which God created for us, he offers us practical advice, which is that we accept the circumstances in which we live and enjoy life as far as possible, looking at everything, even eating and drinking and the ability to work and toil, as a divine gift, since God has given us this life and has planned it as it is.
"There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul see (taste) good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God" [24].

He does not say let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die, as the Stoics, lovers of pleasures, said, but rather let us eat, drink and work giving thanks to God, who gives us everything, even the possibility of eating, drinking and working.

He does not push us toward "escapism," that is, escaping from responsibilities and real troubles by plunging into pleasures and a life of amusement and fantasy, like drug addiction, but urges us to practice real life, giving thanks to God.

St. Augustine sees that the Preacher invites us to the fellowship of the table of the Eucharist, which the Lord Christ instituted with His body and blood given for us, as the Mediator of the New Covenant and the Priest after the order of Melchizedek, so that we eat and drink in a spirit of thanksgiving.

We can say that the Preacher, in this chapter, while affirming the vanity of temporal pleasures, invites us to go out of the world, not going out in the body but in the heart, so that we may not be entangled in its cares nor absorbed by its pleasures, but depart to the age to come with thanksgiving and joy.

* No one draws near to God except the one who has separated himself from the world; but by separation I do not mean departing from the body, but departing from (entanglement) in the affairs of the world.
* Blessed is he who has not lost his way of life in this vain world and on this great sea!
Blessed is the man whose ship has not been wrecked, and who has reached the harbor with joy.

St. Isaac the Syrian His call to us to enjoy the pleasures of ordinary life given by God confirms the Preacher's view of creation, that it is good, and that its vanity depends on our wrong view of it or our misuse of it.
* Idle wealth is of no use, but it becomes fertile and fruitful if its use is regulated.

* Creatures are not evil by their nature; had they been evil, God would not have created them, since every creature of God is good, as the Apostle Paul said (1 Tim 4:4), and His commandment does not order us to reject good things and flee from them, but to manage them well; and no one is condemned for owning wealth, but for boasting of it or for misusing it.
St. Basil the Great The Preacher's words here are an invitation to a life of joyful work, for he says:
"There is nothing better for a man than that... he should make his soul see good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God" [24].

If we thank God for the food and drink He has given us, we thank Him also because He has granted us to toil, working with pleasure and joy, working not only in the life of worship but in our ordinary daily life. St. Basil the Great has delightful discourses on "work," even for monks.

* Since our Lord Jesus Christ said, "The worker is worthy of his wages" (Mt 10:10), and not just anyone at all and anyhow, and the Apostle commanded us to toil and to work with our hands what is good so that we may have something to share with the needy (Eph 4:28), it is therefore clear that we must work diligently, for it is not permitted to us to make worship a pretext for idleness and for fleeing from toil...

And since some disdain work on the pretext of prayers and singing psalms, such people should know that everything has its own time, as the Preacher said: "To every thing there is a season" (Eccl 3:1).

* The prohibition of excessive care for the needs of our body does not negate care and work altogether. For it remains for us "to work for ourselves, not for the food which perisheth, but for the food which endureth unto everlasting life" (Jn 6:27). And the Lord will say to us on the Day of Judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink" (Mt 25:35, etc.). And on the contrary, He will punish those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and to serve their neighbor (Acts 20:4), and will send them to torment (Mt 25:21). Work, then, on this understanding, orders social relations in the best way and gives them an atmosphere of mutual support and harmony.

* Everyone must attend to his own particular work and care for it willingly and fulfil it blamelessly with zeal, diligence, care and watchfulness, lest he deserve the curse, for it is said: "Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord slackly" (Jer 48:10)...

It is better for us to undertake one work with discipline and precision than to do many works without finish. For distraction among many occupations and moving from one thing to another so that none of them is accomplished is a sign of a levity rooted in nature or a cause of the generation of that levity.
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: 1 To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: 2 A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; 3 A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; 4 A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; 5 A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; 6 A time to get, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; 7 A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; 8 A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. 9 What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth? 10 I have seen the travail which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it.
"To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" [1].

Our life, with all its circumstances and conditions, proceeds according to an ordered schedule that fulfils God's purposes at the right time. We must perform our duties faithfully and prepare for the future, that we may see God's plan for us. By a divine plan God created the world for our sake, and at the right time He sent the fathers and the prophets and gave us the Law, and at the appointed time salvation was accomplished by the Cross, and by heavenly wisdom God cares for every small and great thing in your life, so that even the number of the hairs of your head does not escape His care.

In other words, the history of the whole world, and the history of your own life in particular, with all its details, are links in a chain of events that God arranges... You must live in a spirit of faithfulness, working with all your energies and living with joy and gladness, trusting in God who orders your life; for by yourself you cannot do anything, whatever your desire and whatever your abilities... for "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" [1].
a. Origen explains how the Law has its time and the covenant of grace has its time, saying:

["To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." There is a time for gathering good pearls, and another time, after gathering them, for discovering the pearl of great price, when it befits a man to go and sell all that he has to buy that pearl. For just as a man who wants to become wise in the words of truth must first learn the principles, and then pass beyond the elementary teaching, which he esteems with all esteem yet does not remain fixed at that point, but honors it at the outset and then seeks perfection. He acknowledges gratitude for what he was first taught, because it benefited him greatly! So he who understands the Law and the Prophets with full mastery knows that they are elementary teaching for grasping the Gospel in its fullness and grasping the meaning of all the words and works of Christ.

Origen b. St. Gregory of Nazianzus was attacked because he asked that speaking about God with others be done wisely, in a suitable manner and at the right time. He defended himself, saying: [I do not forbid the constant remembrance of God, but only speaking about God, not because there is anything wrong in it in itself, but when it is presented in an unreasonable manner; and I do not forbid all teaching but ask for moderation in it. It is like honey: if a man eats it greedily in excess, it causes vomiting, though it is honey. Solomon says: "To every thing there is a season," and in my belief what is good no longer remains good if it is used in a way that is not good. It is like one who plucks a flower out of the winter season, and as a man's garment does not suit a woman, and the opposite is also true. Athletic games do not befit a place of mourning, nor tears a place of merriment; we all do not accept a thing out of its time, while we honor it if it is used at the right time. Is it not so, my friends and brethren?].

c. St. Gregory defended Pope Athanasius the Apostolic, who hid himself in the time of distress, when the Arians tried to kill him, and appeared at the right time, saying: [I approve of Solomon's wise counsel that to every thing there is a season. Therefore he hid himself for a time, fleeing in the time of war, to appear in the time of peace which soon came afterward]. He also defended his own flight when he was accused of defeat, saying: [To every thing there is a season: there is a time for defeat (for flight), and, as I think, a season to every purpose. It is better to be defeated with honor than to win and prevail by a dangerous, unlawful victory].
Wise Solomon presents several examples to confirm that to every thing there is a season:

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: a. "A time to be born, and a time to die" [2]: God in His love for us has fixed the time of our birth and also the time of our departure from this world; this does not mean that we should not care for our bodily life on the pretext that God has appointed the hour of our departure and that our care will be of no avail. The Lord Christ asked His disciples to flee when they were persecuted, not out of fear of death, but for their own safety. The Arians attacked Pope Athanasius because he fled from them when they tried to kill him. In his defense he said: [Father Isaac said to his son Esau, "Behold now, I am old, I know not the day of my death" (Gen 27:2). But our Lord, being God the Word of the Father, knew the time that He Himself appoints for all, and knew the time of His sufferings, which He Himself determined for His body; yet because He became man for our sake, He hid Himself when they sought (to kill Him) before the appointed time came, as we do. And when He was persecuted He fled, avoiding the plots of His enemies, and passed through the midst of them].

If the Lord has fixed the time of our birth and the time of our death, yet He puts on our shoulders the responsibility of caring for our temporal life and the health and safety of our body; He also fixes the time of the death of our old man and the birth of our new man, where the two take place together at one time in Baptism (Rev 6:4-6), and we too are bound to work by the Spirit of God, striving not to live according to the works of the old man but according to the new man.

* In the very same moment you died and were born; and this water of salvation became at once your grave and your mother, and what Solomon said about others has become fitting for you also, for he says, "A time to conceive and a time to die." But for you it happens otherwise, for there is a time to die followed by a time to be born, and the two happen together, since your (spiritual) birth goes side by side with your death.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem Since there is a time for birth, let us prepare to depart, for we do not know the time that God appoints for us; so we live in a world with no stability, not securing our life even for one coming moment.

* You were born, and therefore you die: if you flee from death, or avoid it, or push it away from you, you cannot postpone it or keep it from you. It is bound to come, even if you refuse; and at an hour you do not know...
Since here you cannot wish not to die, choose to be with the living, lest you die forever...
You who do all you can to postpone death a little, do something so that you may not die forever...

St. Augustine b. "A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted" [2]: there is a set time for planting trees and a special time for uprooting them; so also God plants certain nations and allows them authority and power, and also allows them to be uprooted. Nations have arisen of which no one could have thought that they would decline, but in moments God allowed them to collapse, so that man may realize the vanity of the whole world.

The believer realizes that there is a time for planting holy thoughts and a time for uprooting evil and unseemly thoughts, where he learns a life of constant prayer, supplication and perseverance, and reliance on the free grace of God, awaiting the sanctification and purification of his thoughts by the Holy Spirit of God.
Let us be planted like an olive tree in the house of the Lord, and let us be uprooted from the field of this passing world!

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: c. "A time to kill, and a time to heal" [3]: perhaps he meant by this the killing of the old man and the healing of the new man, which is accomplished in the waters of Baptism (Rom 6:4-6).

Perhaps he means that need sometimes requires great firmness in judgment, where a sentence of death is sometimes passed for the edification of the community and to rescue it from those who pose a grave danger to it, and the matter may call for pardon and gentleness.
It is noted here that he begins with killing and follows it with healing, to show that firmness does not carry a spirit of vengeance and anger, but is for edification and healing.
Let us not fear the vanity of the world, for although we see it as a killing of our temporal life, it carries healing for our eternal life. Let us die that we may live in the Lord forever!

d. "A time to break down, and a time to build up" [3]: we must not stop at the negative side: the breaking down of the old man with his works and thoughts, but must extend to the positive side, which is the building up of the inner new man and his virtues. It is not enough, for example, to break down hatred; love must be established.

He begins with breaking down because we cannot set up a lofty building unless we dig the foundations, and as St. Augustine says, by humility we break down the pride of our haughtiness and lay the foundations of the building of the Spirit that rises to the heavens!

He also says: [The medicine for your sickness is the humility of Christ... Do not exalt yourself but humble yourself if you wish to be healed. And if you wish to reach the height of God, seek Him first in His humility... when you take His humility and rise with Him... Look at the tree, how its growth begins from below and then rises into the air. Its roots are in the earth and its branches toward heaven. Can the tree rise into the air if it does not rely on its roots in the earth? If you wish to reach the heavens apart from humility and love, you have no root. Then you seek destruction, not growth...].

The time for breaking down has come, for the Creator of the whole world declares: heaven and earth shall pass away (Mt 5:8), and the time for building comes, where there is a new heaven and a new earth (Rev 21:1) and a new city (Rev 21:2).

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: e. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance" [4]: as we practice weeping over our souls by being crucified with our Lord Jesus Christ, and mourning over our sins, we enjoy the joy of the Resurrection and the gladness (laughter) of the heavenly beings, and the dances of the soul, rejoicing in the work of Christ risen from the dead in us. The psalmist says: "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy (singing) cometh in the morning" (Ps 30:5).

There is a time to weep, for as long as we are in this world, the valley of tears, it befits us to offer constant repentance for our sins and daily weaknesses, so that when the day of the Lord comes there will be no sorrow nor crying nor pain (Rev 21:4).
* If you weep here you receive rest with every consolation, and there, if you weep, you go to torment...
* Weep here a little, lest you weep there forever in the outer darkness...
* Weep when you pray, that you may find rest...
* By tears, Hannah received Samuel the prophet from God...
St. Ephrem the Syrian * Blessed are those who weep for the sake of truth, for through their tears they continually see the face of God.
* He who sees himself dead in sins does not need to learn how to weep.
* There are tears that burn and inflame, and others that gladden and make flourish...

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: St. Isaac the Syrian f. "A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather stones" [5]: the scattering of stones or rolling them on the earth (according to the Septuagint) points to the acceptance of the pagan Gentiles, and as St. Jerome says: [God raised up from the hard stones of the Gentiles children to Abraham, so they became holy stones rolling on the earth (Zech 9:16 LXX)]. If the time has come for the pagan Gentiles to accept the faith and bear witness to the Lord Christ on earth... there will come the time when all the living stones are gathered to reveal the heavenly temple of God, of which it is said: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" (Eph 2:20-21). "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God" (Rev 3:12).
