By faith the spiritual building of the temple of the Lord began with living stones, "to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 2:5), and the completion of the building is accomplished by its revelation on the day of the Lord as a heavenly building that remains forever. In other words, let the world be broken down; in its breaking down our inner building is not broken down, but is revealed in greatest power at the coming of the Lord on the clouds and our entrance into His heavenly glory.

The scattering and gathering of stones point to the demolition of an old building and its replacement by a new one... So if the world with its vanity collapses, we are not troubled, for we enjoy a new world, the abiding city which has the foundations, whose maker and builder is God (Heb 11:1).

The scattering of stones also points to filling up fields by casting stones into them and burying them (2 Kgs 3:19, 25), and the gathering of them points to reclaiming the fields and making them fit for sowing.

Perhaps it means here the demolition of the building of the Old Testament to be replaced by the Church of the New Testament, and the demolition of the field of the old people so that the field of the New Testament may arise, extending to the ends of the world... But the Church will not remain confined to this temporal world; rather she awaits the collapse of the material world and the passing away of what is visible, that we may enjoy what is heavenly and enjoy the invisible God... then we shall see Him face to face.

Stones are also gathered to make a memorial monument as a sign of establishing a covenant between two parties, or as a memorial of great events, like the pillar which Jacob set up (Gen 28:18; 31:52), and the heaps of stones over Achan and Absalom, or for erecting triumphal arches as a sign of victory; and the scattering of stones points to the breaking of the covenant or the removal of memorial triumphal arches.

If by sin the stones of our covenant with God are scattered and the triumphal arches against the enemy of good are torn down, let us hasten and gather the stones by the Spirit of God and renew the covenant in the merits of the Blood, and quickly set up the triumphal arches, for the time is shortened and the days are evil, and the world is ending and passing away.

g. "A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing" [5]. In the previous examples he mostly begins with the painful matter followed by the joyful: he begins with birth followed by death (since the day of departure is sweeter than the day of birth), he begins with killing followed by healing; breaking down followed by building up, weeping followed by laughing, mourning followed by dancing, scattering stones followed by gathering them; so why does he begin here with embracing followed by separation? Is separation better and sweeter? Some Fathers see here a reference to the loftiness of the virgin life; the Old Testament sanctified marriage and urged it as an embrace of love... and everyone awaited the coming of the Messiah, born of woman, hoping he might come from his offspring according to the flesh; then the New Testament came, which, though it sanctified marriage, urges virginity all the more, as a separation from embracing so that the believer may devote all his energies to worship and to witnessing for the joyful Kingdom of God. It is a call not for everyone, but "he that is able to receive it, let him receive it." The Apostle Paul says: "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that... But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord: but he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife" (1 Cor 7:7, 32).

* How shall I explain the great merit and high dignity which the believers and holy virginity have in the sight of God; for the time has come to refrain from embracing. When there is a great multitude from all the nations filling the number of the saints, is there any need to practice the earthly pleasure of the body in order to give offspring?!
* In former times there was a time to embrace, and finally it is a time to refrain from embracing.

* As for the Christians of our age, who have been freed from the bond of marriage, since they have the power to abstain from any bodily relations, they see that the time has come of which it is written, "A time to refrain from embracing," and that it is not the time of embracing; would they not rather choose to preserve their virginity or widowhood?!

St. Augustine This is the symbolic understanding; as for the literal interpretation, it means that those who embrace, that is, the married, will inevitably have their married life dissolved in this world by the death of one of the parties, so that he who married becomes as one who has not married... This is the nature of the vain world, as the Apostle says that those who use it are as though they did not use it, and those who marry as though they did not marry.

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: h. "A time to get (to seek), and a time to lose" [6]: if a man receives temporal blessings, he gives thanks, and if he loses them, he blesses God who gave and took away, saying with righteous Job: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21).

Perhaps getting points to the Old Testament, with its promises of many temporal blessings (Deut 28), and losing to the New Testament, where believers rejoice in the Cross and are glad to give up willingly what they have, counting everything as refuse that they may win Christ (Phil 3:8).
If our coming into the world is a gain as a divine gift, our departure from it is a loss, that we may gain what is greater: the new heaven and the new earth (Rev 21:1)!

i. "A time to keep, and a time to cast away" [6]: there is a time when a thing is kept and man tries to preserve it, but when he feels that repairing it costs him much, he throws it away and gets rid of it to acquire something newer. So we acquire our temporal life and keep it by the Holy Spirit of God, who renews and sanctifies it, but at the right time our temporal life is cast away that we may acquire a higher and more lasting life!

So also man lived in former times under the shadows of the Law and its symbols, keeping it literally like one who preserves pearls; but now that the Lord Christ, the pearl of great price, has come, he casts away the literalism of the Law and leaves the shadows, to live in the fullness of truth, acquiring the new life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: j. "A time to rend, and a time to sew" [7]: perhaps rending points to intensity of grief, for the ancients were accustomed to rend their garments when severe calamities occurred, as Reuben did when he returned and did not find Joseph in the pit (Gen 37:29), and as Job did when his trial grew severe (Job 1:20). And sewing points to joy and the return of peace, for at times of joy all the members of the family take care to sew new clothes fitting for the joy.

Rending also points to our separation from evil habits, and sewing to our attachment to the virtuous, holy life in the Lord. St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [I believe the meaning of the saying "A time to rend, and a time to sew" is that we must separate completely from everything to which we were bound in our evils, and cleave to what is good].
Perhaps rending points to our withdrawal from the wicked who cause stumbling, and sewing to the fellowship of the heavenly beings and the saints in Christ Jesus, the Head of all.
k. "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" [7]: he begins with silence, for it is not fitting to utter a word except after silence and serious thought.

Silence points to the hidden life of contemplation, and speaking points to witnessing to the Savior before others and serving them, for holy silence is not enough; we must also speak the edifying word of the Lord.
* The Preacher mentions first the time that is needed for silence, and then allows a time for speech.
When, then, and in what matters is silence better?

Those who are concerned with conduct say that silence is always better than speech. And Paul distinguishes the times needed for speech and those needed for silence. Sometimes he recommends silence and at other times speech.
When the time for speech comes he says: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" (Eph 4:29).
And he recommends silence, saying: "Let your women keep silence in the churches... And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home" (1 Cor 14:34-35).
He reveals to us the suitable time for speech, saying: "Lie not one to another" (Col 3:9, etc.), "speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25).

St. Gregory of Nyssa * When the mind approaches matters that surpass it, it is a time for deep silence, for it must rather preserve its admiration or amazement at that power which is not grasped or searched out in the depths of our consciences. And realizing that these great men speak not of God's (nature) but of His works, he says: "Who can speak of the mighty acts of the Lord?", "I will shew forth all thy marvellous works," "One generation shall praise thy works to another" (Ps 106:2; 9:1; 145:4)... Thus speaking is of God's (works); but as for approaching His essence, it is a time for silence.

St. Gregory of Nyssa We must be silent in order to contemplate God and enjoy His shining upon us; then we go forth with words of grace, and bear witness to His work in our life and His rich grace and the opening of the door of His Kingdom to every human being. It also befits us not to speak much about divine matters that surpass the mind and cannot be expressed.
The Fathers, through the Gospel mind, advise us to keep stillness and flee from much vain talk, which robs the soul of its calm and its fellowship with God.

As the Fathers warn us of vain talk that spoils the peace of the soul, so they warn us also of vain silence, which is not accompanied by prayer and fellowship with God and vigilance for the sake of the Kingdom.

St. John Chrysostom says that there is good speech and idle speech, as there is good silence and idle silence... We must know when to be silent and when to speak, and how to be silent and about what to speak.
* The more a man flees from chattering with his tongue, the more his mind is enlightened, so that he can sort out and evaluate deep thoughts, because the mind is confused by chatter.
St. Isaac the Syrian * If we are to give account for every idle word, let us be careful not to utter it; and let us also beware of idle silence!

But there is an effective silence, like the silence of Susanna, who by her silence did more than if she had spoken. For by her silence before men, she spoke with God, and she found no stronger proof of her chastity than silence. Her conscience spoke when she found no word to utter, and she did not ask for judgment from men, for she had the Lord's testimony. Therefore she longed that God Himself would acquit her, knowing that He cannot be deceived by any means.
The Lord Himself also worked in silence to accomplish the salvation of mankind.
David asked that his soul not be occupied with rigid silence but with watchfulness and attentiveness.
St. Ambrose * Nevertheless there is a time to speak of those things by which we advance in virtue in our life.

entries.section: 1. To every thing there is a season:

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa l. "A time to love, and a time to hate" [8]: in the meekness of love St. Demiana was submissive to her father Mark, governor of Bruls, and when he denied the faith, with a firmness resembling hatred she told him that if he did not return to the faith by repentance she would not count him her father, nor would she be his daughter.
Let us love everyone in the Lord, and let us be firm so as to seem as if hating, for the sake of our salvation and theirs.

m. "A time of war, and a time of peace" [8]; the matter sometimes needs a firmness that resembles war; then we must know how to reconcile and bind up wounds. Therefore he mentioned peace after war, so that we do not stop at firmness and severity as long as we can. Even if the Church disciplines heretics, she awaits with longing their return to the truth and their reconciliation.

Perhaps the most wonderful example of this is St. Cyril the Great, whom some scholars unfortunately attack as a violent leader against Nestorius; we read in one of his letters to Nestorius that there is no one who loves him as he does.

11 He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set eternity in their heart, without which man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end. 12 I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life. 13 And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God. 14 I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him. 15 That which hath been is of old; and that which is to be hath of old been; and God requireth that which is past.
It is clear from the previous examples that:
a. To every thing there is a season... as though nothing is good in itself, but according to our use of it in the fitting measure and at the fitting time.

* The things we use in certain circumstances and at suitable times, so that they sanctify us... are things that are neither good nor evil, such as marriage, farming, wealth, withdrawal into the desert, vigils, reading Holy Scripture and meditating on it, and fasting... For these things, or some of them, our forefathers commanded us to carry out with discernment, and to pay attention to the motive for them, the place of carrying them out, the means and the time. For when we carry them out in a suitable manner they become good and fitting, and if we use them with deviation they become evil and harmful... Fasting is reckoned evil for those who expect by it the praise of men...
Abba Theonas b. To every thing there is a season... so nothing remains eternal!
c. Since to every thing there is a season, man is unable to grasp God's purposes and His surpassing arrangements and to change them.

d. The previous examples point to God's work with us, for the new time has come in which we have passed from the age of the Law to the age of grace, from the stage of spiritual childhood to maturity, from shadow and letter to truth and spirit, from the time of temporal gains to the joyful loss for the sake of Him who gave His life for us, from the season of strife and enmity with God to reconciliation with Him as members of His household! e. God, who created time and is not subject to it, for the sake of the arrangement of our salvation submitted by His will to time, when He took our nature and accepted death in His body for us.

f. If God, as a Creator who loves mankind, "hath made every thing beautiful in his time" [11], and all that He created is good and well ordered, yet He lifts us above time... He submitted to time in order to lift us above time, for "he hath set eternity in their heart, without which man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end" [11].

The word "eternity" here is one of the words around which most dispute has arisen in the Book of Ecclesiastes. Some have suggested that it is "the universe," others "mystery" or "forgetfulness," and others have reckoned it derived from the Ugaritie root "glm," meaning "becomes dark," saying that God made everything beautiful and fitting but man is unable to grasp the mysteries of God's plan and wisdom because darkness has settled upon his mind and heart.

g. Lest anyone think that the lifting of the heart to heaven or to eternity pushes us into gloom or into contempt for temporal life, he returns to affirm that all we receive or practice with wisdom is a divine gift: "I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life. And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy the good of all his labour, it is the gift of God" [12-13].

The Preacher cannot be accused of any materialistic or hedonistic tendencies, that is, that pleasure or enjoyment is the only good in this worldly life; rather, as we said before, he carries a tendency of praise through which the believer feels that all he has in his hands is a gift of God, even eating and drinking, so he finds enjoyment in life because it bears the imprints of God's surpassing love. He feels that the circumstances he lives in and the resources in his hands are the best that suit him in this life as a preparation for eternal life, so he lives his life in a spirit of praise and joy.

h. "To every thing there is a season": God dealt with the men of the Old Testament as children in faith, urging them to holiness with temporal blessings, while with the men of the New Testament He urges them as men to holiness by bearing the Cross and sharing His sufferings; yet in His dealings, His covenants and His love He has not changed. We change and alter our position toward Him, therefore it is said: "I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it" [14].
And lest it be thought that God's dealings with the Church of the New Testament are at the expense of the men of the Old Testament, he says: "God requireth that which is past" [15].

16 And moreover I saw under the sun that in the place of truth there is injustice, and in the place of justice there is oppression! 17 I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work. 18 I said in mine heart concerning the estate of the sons of men, that God tests them, to show them that they themselves are like a beast. 19 For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for both are vanity. 20 All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. 21 Who knoweth the spirit of the sons of men, whether it goeth upward? and the spirit of the beast, whether it goeth downward to the earth? 22 Wherefore I perceived that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?

If to every thing there is a season [1], and if the good God made every thing beautiful in its time [11], then the corruption that has come upon the world is not from the nature of the world itself, but through man's injustice and oppression of his fellow man.

What witness to the vanity of the world is like injustice occupying the place of truth, and oppression the place of justice [16]? Corruption spreads into the depths of the courts of justice! But the Preacher believes in God's just judgment. The corruption of the world does not mean that things proceed in an arbitrary way without restraint; rather God awaits the right time to judge the righteous and the wicked [17]. "For there is a time there for every purpose and for every work" [17]. In other words, if man by his corruption has wronged the world, in that he did not put everything in its proper time and place, so that injustice occupied the place of justice... yet God intervenes to set the situation right, but also in His own time.
The natural man thinks that man and beast are subject to death with no distinction between them; so does the spirit of man go upward and the spirit of the beast go downward under the earth?

Even if death comes upon the righteous and the wicked, upon man and animal, yet the righteous man, having cleaved to his Creator, does not fear death, which is the last door that separates him from his God.

entries.section: 1. Oppression and the loss of humanity:

paragraphs.text: 1 So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter. 2 Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. 3 Yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.

The Preacher declares that oppression is the mark of all the works of man [1]; the oppressed appear unable to act, and their cry tears the heart of the Preacher. Solomon was so tender in his feelings that he could not bear the tears of the oppressed, counting the dead more blessed than the living who see injustice prevailing in the world, and the miscarriage, which is not born but dies like a child in its mother's womb, more blessed than all, because it "hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun" [3].

The Preacher was not pessimistic in his longing for death; rather he was tender to the utmost, unable to bear the sight of the oppressed, imitating his Lord who says: "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" (Song 6:5)... Perhaps the Preacher himself also feared lest he should share in the oppression and fall prey to it.

St. Ambrose expresses the feelings of the Preacher, who longed for death rather than see injustice, saying: [The Preacher affirms that one born dead is better than one advanced in age, because he has not seen the evils that have befallen this world. He has not come into that darkness, nor walked in the vanity of the world; therefore he who has not come into this life is more at rest than he who has come into it. Truly, what is the good of man in this life? He lives in darkness and is not satisfied in his desires, and when he is gorged with riches he lacks rest, since he is bound to guard the possessions he has acquired because of his wicked greed. Because he acquired that property by gluttony and covetousness, he sees that it gives him no good. How bitter it is that a man should guard his possessions and be tormented and not profit by their abundance!].

If the Preacher praises one who died in his mother's womb so that he might not see injustice, or might not share in men's injustice, covetousness and greed, should we not all the more call blessed the one who dies of his own free will with his crucified Christ, out of love for God and men? As Origen says: [Who is to be praised with more worthiness than he who dies in the full freedom of his will for the sake of his religion (his faith)?!].

4 Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit. 5 The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh. 6 Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.

The Preacher criticizes those who rely on idleness and the seeking of ease, either because they feel the injustice around them and are overcome by frustration, asking: What have those who acquired abundant riches gained? Or because, in practicing injustice, they seek to grow rich at the expense of their brethren, and so they seek ease in relaxation in order to reap the fruit of the labor of others. In any case the Preacher asks the believers for a life of moderation, without extremes either toward slackness and idleness or toward exaggeration in seeking wealth and possessions.
"Again, I considered all travail, and every right work (success), that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit" [4].

What man thinks to be success in his work, when he gathers and hoards, comparing himself with others and envying his neighbor who acquires more than he, is vanity and a seizing of the wind... for it corrupts man's inner nature, driving it to practice injustice and oppression instead of love and mercy. St. Gregory the Wonder-worker says: [It has also become clear to me how dangerous is the envy that afflicts a man toward his neighbor like the sting of an evil spirit, and I have seen that he who falls prey to it, and whose breast is filled with it, can do nothing but eat and tear his own heart! His soul collapses and his body wastes away, for he finds no comfort in the good things of others].

St. Basil the Great says: [There is no passion worse or more harmful than envy. It does not harm the neighbor so much as it harms the envious man himself. Envy is a worm that gnaws in the depths of man's heart, and works in it as rust works on iron. It is dejection of soul and grief that befalls a man at the sight of the happiness others enjoy... The worst thing about envy is that it is a sickness that is kept hidden. You see the envious man with lowered gaze and sullen face, constantly complaining of inner torment, which withers his face and wears out his body, so that he grows thin and weak. He is ashamed to say: "I am envious," I feel bitterness and sorrow at the good that another man has obtained, I am tormented by the happiness of my friends, and I cannot bear the success of my peers. I see that the happiness of others is a sword that tears my bowels and pierces me to the heart...

The envious man, besides what we have mentioned, loses the right sense and feeling for values... With him virtue becomes vice, and good becomes evil. Thus the brave man is considered by the envious to be rash, the prudent dull, the righteous a criminal, the wise a hypocrite, the generous wasteful and prodigal, and the thrifty miserly. All virtues become vices in the eyes of the envious].
"The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh" [5].

The idle man, whether fleeing from the injustice of others or intending to benefit from the labor of others without sharing their work, gains nothing. He folds his hands from work, and so loses everything and finds not even what to eat... so he eats his own flesh. This is a figurative expression meaning to die of hunger, or meaning that the idle man enters a state of inner emptiness; instead of thinking of positive work he is confused by many exaggerated thoughts, which destroy his psychological state and rob him of his health, even his bodily health.

* There is no need for me to describe to you the gravity of the evil of idleness, when the Apostle commanded plainly: "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10). For as daily food is necessary for every man, so toil according to his strength is necessary for him. Solomon did not write in vain, in praise of the diligent woman: "[she] eateth not the bread of idleness" (Prov 31:27), as the Apostle also said of himself: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day" (2 Thess 3:8), although he had the authority, as a preacher of the Gospel, to live of the Gospel (1 Cor 9:14); indeed the Lord (in His discourse) joined idleness with evil, when He said: "Thou wicked and slothful servant" (Mt 25:26). Moreover, wise Solomon did not only commend the worker as we have mentioned (Prov 31:27) but rebuked the idle man by likening him to the lowest of creatures (the insects), saying: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard" (Prov 6:6). Therefore we must fear lest we too be rebuked on the day of judgment, because He who gave us the ability to work asks of us works that suit this ability, for He said: "To whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more" (Lk 12:48).

And since some shrink from work on the pretext of prayers and the chanting of the Psalms, such people must know that for everything there is its own time, as the Preacher said: "To every thing there is a season" (Eccl 3:1).
St. Basil the Great "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit" [6].

It is better for a man to work so as to enjoy a handful with ease of heart and peace of soul than to venture violently in envy and zeal for the sake of hoarding and abundance of riches, and so actually gain a double yield but with anxiety and disturbance; for in reality he reaps the anxiety that crushes him, that is, he reaps a seizing of the wind. St. Paul says his final word on this: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:11-13).

In the Conferences of St. John Cassian, Abba Abraham sees that the words of wise Solomon here explain the superiority of quiet work in the wilderness, with some inner rest and security, over care for serving others while being immersed with them in their material affairs, for he says: [It is better for us to persevere constantly in our purpose, acquiring a moderate gain in the wilderness, where there are no worldly cares or entanglements that scatter the mind, no pride and no vainglory, and where the cares of daily necessities are fewer... This is better than seeking great gain through conversing with others in a most profitable discourse, while we become immersed in the demands of secular life, which is full of daily entanglements. For Solomon says: "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit." In these snares the weak fall... for while they are careless of their own salvation, and while they themselves need the teaching and guidance of others, they are deceived by the wiles of Satan under the cover of bringing others to repentance and guiding them].

7 Then I returned, and I saw vanity under the sun. 8 There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail. 9 Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. 10 For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up. 11 Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone? 12 And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

The Preacher reveals the folly of the oppressors from many sides. The oppressor, in his love of acquiring and hoarding, envies his neighbor for what he has, and so loses his inner peace... He remains in a state of constant hunger however much wealth he gains [4]. Injustice may drive him to slackness and idleness, that he may unjustly reap the fruits of his neighbor, and while he is in slackness and idleness he finds that he eats his own flesh, and so does not enjoy true rest [5]. Or he may go to another extreme, working without limits in order to acquire manifold wealth, and then he reaps only toil and a seizing of the wind [6]. Finally, his selfishness may drive him into a state of extreme misery when he is cut off from the company of others, sacrificing every friendship and every love of sharing for the sake of hoarding wealth, which the Preacher expressed, saying:

"Then I returned, and I saw vanity under the sun. There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches" [7-8].

He gives an example: a man isolated in selfishness even from his brothers and his sons, as though he had no brothers and no sons. He gathers much, but he deprives himself, as he deprives those nearest to him, of meeting in the circle of love, and he does not know what will be the end of what he gathers!

How bitter I felt while I was in the United States when I learned that a man and his son had resorted to the courts, each claiming ownership of a project in which they had shared and which had brought abundant profit... The love of money destroys even fatherhood and sonship! Can money satisfy the heart of a man who isolates himself from everyone, even from his son?!
* One who is left alone in harsh isolation, without brother or son, yet possesses a vast and rich estate, lives in greedy gluttony and refuses to give himself to any good work!

The gravest calamity of the man who owns vain wealth (in covetousness) is his lack of a friend to help him and bring gladness to his heart. But those who live together multiply the good wealth that falls into their hands, and their fellowship lessens the pressure of the storms of hateful events. For by day they are distinguished by their strong trust in one another, and by night they are marked by cheerfulness and patience. But he who lives a life of isolation is filled with dread...

St. Gregory the Wonder-worker If injustice drives a man to isolation, so that for one reason or another he cannot bear true fellowship, therefore the Preacher urges us to practice a life of fellowship, team work and active, effective friendship, saying:
"Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.
But woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" [9-10].
Relying on these words, St. Pachomius made it a rule that no monk should dwell alone in a cell.
Working friendship has its effectiveness and is necessary in the life of faith, and as the Jewish proverb in the Talmud says: "Either companionship or death."
* I always long to form close relationships with the righteous, and I am often moved to love them. For we read: "Two are better than one... if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" [9].
St. Jerome * The lover of the saints is a companion of the angels.
* Let your conversation be with those who love God, that your soul may take on the likeness of their purity.

St. John Saba Church history tells us of wonderful examples of friendships and the spiritual blessings they brought into the lives of the saints. We mention, for example, the friendship that arose between St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, of whom the latter says: [I breathe you in more than I breathe the air, and whether I am present or absent, I live only the time in which you are with me]. He also says: [When we became acquainted and our common desire to study true philosophy became clear, each of us became everything to the other. We had one roof over our house and one table at which we studied, and shared sentiments. Our eyes soared toward one goal, and our affection only grew and became firmer day by day. Bodily passions pass away, but the love that has a bond with God is steadfast because its place is steadfast, and the more its beauties become clear and are revealed, the more it binds together those whom it has joined in the same bond of love].
And St. Basil offers us his experience of this friendship, saying:
[In life in community a man does not enjoy only his own particular gift, but multiplies it by sharing it with others, and gathers fruit from their gifts as he gathers from his own gift].
[But the man who hides in himself the graces and gifts God has granted him, and does not share their benefits with others, is condemned like one who buried his talent].

Some of the Fathers see in the Preacher's saying, "Two are better than one," a confirmation of the necessity of a spiritual father who supports the believer lest he deviate according to his own self-will.

* Many desire virginity while they are still young and of little understanding; these must be occupied before everything with seeking a suitable guide and teacher for this way, lest in their present ignorance they turn aside from the right way and fall into another road, rugged in its paths, of their own devising. "Two are better than one," so says the wise man, for it is easy for one to be defeated at the hands of the adversary who sets his snares on the road that leads to God; and truly "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

St. Gregory of Nyssa On the other hand, it befits each of us to be concerned to raise up his brother in a spirit of meekness and love, as the Preacher says: "If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" [9].

* In practicing the work of the Preacher, set before your eyes that you direct your life well, and that you pray for the foolish that they may gain understanding and know how to cease from evil deeds.
St. Gregory the Wonder-worker The Preacher offers us examples to confirm the importance of friendship and spiritual fellowship for edification:
The first example: "If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?!"

He means those who lie together to keep each other warm, travelers in desert regions bitterly cold at night who do not have sufficient coverings; or perhaps he means a good married life, which grants family warmth and satisfaction within the soul in the Lord.

The second example: "And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken" [12]. That is, if friendship and partnership with another gives a man strength, so that if one attacks him two stand against him, what then if the fellowship is among three? Cords woven of three strands endure more than those woven of two.

What is this threefold cord but the unity of the Church community, in whose midst the Lord Christ dwells according to His promise: "If two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them"? St. Jerome sees that it represents the bond between faith, hope and love, saying: [The words of the Apostle about faith, hope and love are like the threefold cord that is not easily broken. We believe and we hope, and through our faith and our hope we are bound to one another with the bond of love].

13 Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. 14 For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor. 15 I considered all the living which walk under the sun, with the second child that shall stand up in his stead. 16 There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit.

Having presented the Preacher's testimony about the vanity of the world, where injustice prevails over mankind and takes the place of justice, and because of which some in folly seek ease at the expense of others, their hearts inflamed with envy and jealousy, while others withdraw into themselves in selfishness instead of working together as a team in a spirit of sharing and love, many also spoil their labor by seeking vainglory and temporal honor at any cost; yet this honor depends on the fluctuations of men and is therefore without security... A prisoner may come out to the throne, and a king may descend to prison.

Man's true greatness is not in the multitude of his days, nor in his position or his abilities, but in the wisdom that dwells in him: "Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished" [13]... He is a king of many days with all abilities, but by lacking wisdom he lacks a life of watchfulness.

He affirms that conditions do not last; a man may come out of prison to the throne, like Joseph, and a king may be driven from his throne [14]. The first gains the love of men while the second is hated. Perhaps by the one who comes out of prison he meant man himself, for he was born from his mother's womb naked, as one in a prison, only to find himself occupying the throne without struggle or skill or abilities of his own or any personal privilege of his own.

The one who comes out of prison to the kingdom points to the men of the New Testament who are freed from the prison of the letter of the Law, and the deposed king is the Jews, who have in their hands the Law and the prophecies and the divine promises but denied faith in the Savior. By the letter the leaders of the Jews lost the kingdom, and by faith the believers became kings and priests (Rev 1:6) in the life of Baptism.

When the Jewish leader, literal in worship, loses his spiritual kingship, the people gathered around him leave him to enjoy the work of faith in Christ, the Giver of the kingdom, and the true believers also do not rejoice in him [16].

Origen sees that the one who comes out of prison to the kingdom is the martyr who goes forth to the King of kings to enjoy a lasting throne that is not taken from him, for he says: ["Out of prison he cometh to reign." Thus I was persuaded to die for the truth, despising at once what is called death. Bring the fierce beasts, bring the crosses, offer the fires, come, you tormentors. I know that when I die I go out of my body and rest with Christ].

Thus, as the Preacher used the testimony of society in the world and the injustice it bears because of the selfishness of some of the rich and those in authority, he calls all to a spirit of love and sharing, far from the seeking of vainglory.

1 Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil. 2 Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few. 3 For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words. 4 When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. 5 Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. 6 Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands? 7 For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God.

If the world apart from God is vanity and a seizing of the wind, then all the more is formal worship outside the sphere of the Spirit vanity and a seizing of the wind. Here the Preacher begins to apply our sincere view of life to worship, whether communal or private.
a. A call to enter the house of God:
"Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil" [1].

God created the world good, that the whole earth might be like the house of God, in which every man would meet his beloved, holy Creator in a spirit of love, praise and joy. But when sin entered the world the world became vanity, the earth brought forth thorns and thistles, and man felt a dryness toward his good Creator. Yet God, in His love for man, allowed him to build a house for Him as an icon of the eternal heaven, to which the believers may flee while they are still in this world, so that the Spirit of God carries their hearts, thoughts, wills, feelings and senses to what is above the visible world and above time... Therefore we do not wonder that the Preacher, after affirming the vanity of the world, began his counsels to man with going to the house of God. In other words the Preacher says: Flee from the passing world to its eternal Creator by entering His holy house and meeting Him in the sphere of love and obedience.
The Psalmist knew how to flee to God's sanctuaries in times of distress, to experience God's mercies and the riches of His grace:
"Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever" (Ps 23:6).

"Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident. One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple" (Ps 27:3-4).
"For thou hast been a shelter for me... I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings" (Ps 61:3-4).
"All the day long have I been plagued... Until I went into the sanctuary of God" (Ps 73:14, 17).

Thus when the Psalmist felt troubles, outward or inward, he found a refuge in the house of the Lord, where he meets God Himself, his Savior. He lifts him up to His graces and grants him the experience of the beauty of the heavenly life, so that he is no longer occupied with the afflictions that time brought him. In the house of the Lord he finds God the King seated on the throne, so he does not fear if a host encamps against him or war rises against him!

However, entering the house of the Lord and dwelling in it requires purity and holiness of heart, so that the believer may dwell with the holy God in His sanctuary and have fellowship with Him... Therefore he says: "Keep thy foot" [1].

b. What does keeping the foot when going to the house of the Lord mean, but what the wise man says: "The prudent man looketh well to his going" (Prov 14:15), and also: "Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established. Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil" (Prov 4:26). It is as though he says: You are walking the royal road to enter the throne of the King of kings; take care lest you swerve by a blow from the right, that is, by self-righteousness, or by a blow from the left, that is, by falling into evil. Enter the house of the Lord with your heart before your body... Do not hasten with the steps of your bodily feet, but enter with your depths, led by the Holy Spirit of God.

Some see in this commandment, "Keep thy foot," a reference to God's command to the prophet Moses and to Joshua the son of Nun to take off their shoes from their feet (Ex 3:5; Josh 5:15), and as Origen says, it is a call to take off the shoe made of the skin of dead animals. We put off from us whatever touches the dead life, or the works of the old man, that we may live by the Spirit of God in newness of life. Also it is made from the skin of drums, which give a loud sound without work, as though the taking off of the skin were a call to reject vainglory and the love of display...

Let us enter the house of the Lord with our hearts after taking the shoes off them, that we may enjoy the works of the new man, so that we do not walk in the evil life nor seek self-righteousness, but listen to the voice of God and obey Him with a holy and pure will, for to hear God is better than the sacrifice of fools!

c. To hear is better than the sacrifice of fools: Keep your heart, or your inner man, in obedience, as the eye that beholds God by faith, and the foot by which you walk toward Him and enjoy your dwelling with Him and His dwelling with you.

If life is changing and passing away, and needs vigilance and caution lest you fall into the snares of being entangled in it and tempted to hoard its temporal goods, then all the more, when you turn your heart toward the house of God, you come to know the royal road, the road of obedience to Christ, for to walk by it and in it is greater than offering material gifts to the house of the Lord. Receive the Lord Christ Himself as a royal road, and so bear His righteousness and obedience, offering your heart as a sacrifice of practical love... for God asks for your heart, not your money! And as you give Him your heart poured out in practical love, through your union with the obedient Christ (Heb 5:5), you offer all your life, its greater and lesser sins.

He asks us to hear, for the house of God is the house of the divine Word; we hear Him that we may keep Him within us by His Holy Spirit. The first word in the Ten Commandments is "Hear"... for God wants us to enter His house to listen, and to have it kept in the heart and in practical conduct, because hearing means practical obedience.

God, as we know Him in the Holy Bible and in the experience of the Church throughout the ages, is the "Hearer of prayers"; He inclines His ear to us, His children, to hear the whispers of our lips and the hidden sighs of our hearts, and we, in our love for Him, answer His listening to us with our listening to Him... We share with Him the quality of "hearing." In His love He comes down to us to hear us, and in His love He also grants us the spirit of obedience so that we hear Him!

Hearing (obedience) is not a kind of humiliation, as some think in the pride of their hearts, but it is the mark of the true believer in his fellowship with God who hears our voices... We hear Him in His commandment as in His house, in our hidden prayers and in our dealings with our neighbor... We bear the mark of hearing as a holy nature in the Lord that accompanies us in our closet, in our church, in our homes, in our work, even on the road; we long to hear everyone and obey him, but in the Lord!

Finally, by hearing he calls us to heavenly wisdom and a walk in the righteousness of God; wisdom is bound to righteousness as folly is bound to evil, for he says: "the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil." The fool not only sins but sins without caring, whereas the wise man, if he sins, cannot bear his sinful conduct, but accuses himself before God in repentance, asking Him to grant him in practice the mark of "hearing" or "obedience."

God rejects the sacrifice of fools because, while they practice the formalities of worship, they refuse to listen inwardly to God's commandments, so that evil reigns over their heart and mind and they do not care about it.
* Upon him who hears and obeys, holy peace descends.

St. John Saba We can sense how our fathers feared falling under the letter of formalities from what St. John Saba said: [O man of God, how long will only the black (the monastic habit) comfort your soul? Be wholly a flame, and burn those around you, that you may see the beauty hidden within you]. And St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian says: [The garb of good religion is put upon me, but its power is not in me]. [I stand in the front of the church, and I am not worthy to be last in it]. [I withdrew from the world, and I am sunk in it up to my neck in my heart and mind].

d. Not multiplying vain words during prayer: "Therefore let thy words be few" [2], for God asks for work and sincerity, not a multitude of vain words" (Mt 6:7). "For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" [3].

Let our prayers be calm, uttered without haste, uttered by our tongue as by our practical life, so that our whole being cries out in the language of practical love, which God listens to and all heaven rejoices in. Perhaps for this reason he says: "Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth" [2]. It is as though he says: Let your life, which is marked by heavenliness, speak and pray, so that the words of prayer rise with it to the divine throne.

Perhaps the Preacher wanted the worshiper not to hurry through the words to finish his prayer, but from time to time to lift his mind, heart and feelings toward God, expressing by inward contemplation the depth of his clinging to Him, and in this way leaving room for the grace of God to work in him during prayer... He speaks in the Spirit, listens to the voice of the Lord and sees in the Spirit. Prayer becomes a dialogue of mutual love in which man shares not with his tongue alone but with his whole inner being.

He says: "For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth"... Wait in your prayers for the Heavenly One to reveal to you His heavens, to teach you the language of heaven, and to grant you fellowship in praise with the heavenly ones.

* Listen to the counsel of the Preacher: Utter not a word before God; for he says that God is in heaven and you are on earth [2]. I believe that by that distance which separates heaven from earth, despite the intimacy of their mutual communion, he shows the nature of God, which immeasurably surpasses the sphere of man's thought. As the stars are far beyond the reach of the fingers, so, and by a far greater degree, that nature which is above all the thoughts of men rises above our earthly thoughts.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * Silence your tongue that your heart may speak, silence your heart that the Spirit may speak in you.

St. John Saba The Preacher calls us not to multiply words in prayer, perhaps so that we may not utter unintelligible words, as the Apostle Paul says: "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also" (1 Cor 14:15). When we pray or praise God we must speak with deliberation and reverence, aware that we are speaking with the Heavenly One...

The Preacher does not attack long prayers as long as they are offered with understanding, wisdom and godliness, for the Lord Christ sometimes spent the whole night in prayer (Lk 6:12), and the Apostle asks us to pray without ceasing (1 Thess 5:17), and to pray always (Col 1:3). And it is said of St. Arsenius that he was absorbed in prayer from sunset until sunrise, spending the whole night in the sweetness of converse with God.
* Pray and do not grow weary; pray continually a prayer of faith, hope and love...
But let not your prayer be in a multitude of words. Our Lord is the first who shortened long speeches, so that in your long prayer to God you may not appear as one who goes on to give Him a lesson.
What you need in prayer is godliness, not babbling.

When you pray, do not be a babbler like the heathen, who think that they shall be heard for their much speaking (Mt 6:7); be not like them, for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask Him...
You will not cease from prayer if you continually seek the happy life...
It is said that in Egypt there are brethren who continually offer short petitions recited quickly, in order to preserve the attention (concentration of mind) necessary for everyone who prays.

St. Augustine The Preacher cites an example that affirms the importance of work over a multitude of words: "For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" [3]. Continuous, earnest work engenders happy dreams, or fulfills man's dreams and desires, but the idle talk of many words turns man's life to folly, his words being "a fool's voice." Much business makes a man wise and realistic even in his dreams, while a multitude of words reveals emptiness and folly!
e. Seriousness and sincerity in vows:
"When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools...
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin" [4-6].

In our study of the books of Numbers (chapter 30) and Leviticus (chapter 27): (Num 30; Lev 27) we spoke about vows in the Mosaic Law. A vow is a promise to consecrate something to God, which a man is bound to fulfill; it points to an inward longing and a sure desire not for consecrating things but for consecrating the heart itself to God, for the glory of His name and the spread of His Kingdom. It befits the believer to keep what he has uttered and not to break his word (Lev 27:2; Judg 11:35), nor is it fitting to put it off until tomorrow.

The Preacher calls those who do not pay their vows or who delay the payment "fools," because they speak foolishly without deliberation, and this is counted a kind of contempt for God. It would have been better for them not to vow than to vow and not pay, so that they would not be counted as breakers of a promise.

They speak with their mouth and their flesh sins. Here the flesh means the whole man. Ananias and Sapphira vowed to give the whole price of their field... but they kept back part of the price, and were counted as having lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:1-11). Jephthah was hasty in his vow to the Lord to offer as a burnt offering whoever came forth from the doors of his house to meet him... and he offered his only daughter, a virgin, as a burnt offering (Judg 11:30, 34). And Herod promised hastily to give Herodias her request even up to half the kingdom, and the head of St. John the Baptist was cut off!
Let us not be hasty in our promises and vows to God and to men!

Abba Isaac, in his Conferences with St. John Cassian, sees that the vow is "prayer," saying thus: [If you have offered a prayer to the Lord, do not delay to fulfill it. And we pray when we renounce this world and promise that we will die to all worldly deeds and to the life of this world, and serve the Lord with all the purposes of the heart].

Our prayers are vows or pledges... in them we declare our renunciation of the pleasures of the world and our acceptance of the Kingdom of God within us, in them we reject the destructive fatherhood of the devil and accept God's fatherhood to us... Let us fulfill this not in words only but in our practical life by the Holy Spirit of God who works in us, so that we may say with power with the Apostle: "We are not of the night, nor of darkness" (1 Thess 5:5).

In our study of the Book of Psalms we noticed that the Psalmist declares his paying of vows by praising God, for there is no vow that gladdens the heart of God like our praising Him and giving Him thanks in the midst of our afflictions and troubles! By this vow we declare that our heavenly God alone is able to bring us into the joyful angelic life and to carry us over the cares and preoccupations of the world!
The Preacher continues his discourse on the obligation to fulfill the vow, saying:
"Neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error" [6].

He means by the angel here the priest (Rev 2:1), for it does not befit the believer to contrive excuses before God's stewards, claiming that what he uttered he did not mean, or that he did not know the truth of his abilities or capacities. For God is angry with those who are hasty in their words and vows [6].
The writer gives the cause of this sickness and its remedy, saying:
"For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God" [7].
St. Gregory the Wonder-worker says: [As a throng of dreams is vain, so is a multitude of words. But the fear of God is man's salvation, though it is hard to acquire].

Three things spoil the pledges of our mouth to God: a multitude of dreams, that is, being occupied with illusions without practical, realistic conduct; vanities, that is, being occupied with the affairs of vain life; and a multitude of words. In other words, for our pledges to be holy and realistic we must flee from vain thoughts (dreams), from vain deeds, and from vain words, by setting the fear of God before our eyes when we think, work or speak. Let us fear God, and He will reign over our thoughts, our conduct and our words... and we shall be, in our whole being, witnesses of truth to His work in us!

8 If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they. 9 Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field. 10 He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity. 11 When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes? 12 The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. 13 There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. 14 But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand. 15 As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand. 16 And this also is a sore evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go: and what profit hath he that hath laboured for the wind? 17 All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he hath much sorrow and wrath with his sickness.

He asked us for true spiritual worship in the face of the vanity of the world, warning us against dry, literal formalities, and offering us the fear of God as a remedy for our weakness in worship. Now he ties spiritual worship to practical conduct filled with sincere love, offering us also the fear of God as our support so that we do not fear the oppressors, for he says:

a. "If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they" [8].

May we not marvel at the matter when we see injustice prevailing on the earth, for over against it there is a comforting sight in heaven. God, who is higher than every throne and above every authority, will surely carry out His care for the oppressed and His justice at the right time. If the oppressors are exalted, the glory of God is above the heavens (Ps 113).

Perhaps the Preacher feared lest the believer marvel at the sight of injustice prevailing on the earth and himself yield to vanity and walk in a spirit of injustice and oppression, on the pretext that the whole world walks so. Rather he should turn to the one who is higher, that is, to the judges or rulers, and if he finds no one on earth to do justice to the poor and the oppressed, the Heavenly One Himself, higher than all, intervenes.

b. If the poor man has become like the earth we do not despise him, for all need him, even the king needs the service of the field and its fruit: "Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field" [9]. All living creation needs the earth... from it the beasts eat, and from it the king eats... so why do we despise it?!

Let us give love to our poor brethren and not despise them, even if they have become in the eyes of many earth that they tread on with their feet, for by our love for them and our service to them we ourselves are served and our heart is lifted up to heaven itself!

c. Let us love the poor and oppressed brethren even if they have become earth, because they will serve us on the great day of the Lord when we hear: "Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40). We give them our silver and our possessions, or rather our love, and so we profit eternally; but if we hoard our possessions our souls are not satisfied [10], and we do not profit by them [11], they give us no rest [12], but may even harm us [13]... and they are passing... for they leave us [14] or we leave them against our will [15-16].

entries.section: First: The love of silver is not satisfying:

paragraphs.text: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase" [10].

He who cleaves to the Lord through godliness profits greatly: "Godliness with contentment is great gain" (1 Tim 6:6), and as the Apostle says: "every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full..." (Phil 4:18). But he who cleaves to the love of riches and wealth enlarges his soul like hell (Hab 2:5), and the whole world cannot satisfy it. It is like the horseleach, a worm that abounds in marshes and attaches itself to animals, drinking from the marshes and sucking the blood of the animals, clinging very closely to them, which says, "Give, give" (Prov 30:15).
* He who loves riches dreams of gold when he sleeps, but to him who loves detachment (the gold) hastens...
* The sons of the Kingdom tread on gold like dust, and you now rejoice and do not carry it...
* O Lord, he who possesses You, the bread of the day, has no need, for he is richer than all the rich of the whole world.
St. Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: Second: Abundance of riches brings no profit:

paragraphs.text: "When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes?! [11].

As a man grows richer his responsibilities grow, so what does he profit if his heart remains greedy for the love of money while those who work with him eat with gladness and joy?! In other words, while the heart of the rich man burns with the lust for riches and the spirit of covetousness, those who live from his goods are happier than he... they may gain their souls and enjoy eternal riches, while he loses his soul?! Let us give them our love, that we also may profit, and our love for them becomes our eternal wealth.
* Be without greed and do not be without mercy. If you are the master of gold, not its servant, you use it well... Greed makes you a slave, and love makes you free.
St. Augustine

entries.section: Third: The love of riches robs us of rest:

paragraphs.text: When he compared the rich man, whose heart is not satisfied with the abundance of his goods, with his workers, he found that the workers eat of the goods by their wages, while the rich man may deprive himself of the goods because of his stinginess and love of acquiring, or the workers may enjoy the eating of heavenly food through their godly life while the stingy rich man is deprived of the heavenly table... Someone may say: But the workers toil and labor, while the rich man in ease reaps the fruit of their labor. The Preacher comments on this by saying that although the poor workers labor in body, they enjoy pleasure when they sleep, regardless of the kind of food they eat or its amount, but the greedy rich man's heart finds no rest at night... Sleep flies from his eyes as he thinks how to multiply his wealth... Therefore it was rightly said: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Ps 127:2).
"The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep" [12].
The worker earns his living by toil but sleeps deeply and with pleasure, while being occupied with multiplying wealth brings cares and anxiety...

* The poor man, even if he is a slave and unable to fill his belly completely, at least enjoys the refreshment of sleep, but the lust of the rich man is always accompanied by insomnia, sleepless nights and tension of mind. What is more foolish than this...?!

St. Gregory the Wonder-worker * The Preacher sees that riches cause their owner troubles, for losing them causes him great anxiety and tension. They are truly as good as lost, for they are left behind here, and are of no use to the dead.

St. Ambrose If bodily toil for the necessities of the body gives pleasure to the body at night, how much more does the one who strives spiritually enjoy true pleasure when he labors for the salvation of his soul?! He truly sleeps the sleep of death in sweetness and delight, for he rests from his labors and his works follow him (Rev 14:13).

* As sheaves of joy follow those who sow in tears, so joy follows those who have endured hardships for God's sake. Bread gained with much sweat seems sweet to the sowers, and sweet are the works of righteousness to the heart that has received the knowledge of Christ.

Mar Isaac the Syrian While he warns us throughout the Book against hoarding or greed, he wishes to affirm that it is also not fitting for us to live in slackness and sluggishness, but to work and strive in our daily life as in our worship, for "the sleep of a labouring man is sweet" [12].

entries.section: Fourth: The love of riches or hoarding is harmful:

paragraphs.text: "There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun.
Namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt" [13].

The evil the wise man saw under the sun is that a rich man devotes himself to guarding his wealth, and behold it harms him, as he says in another place: "So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof" (Prov 1:19). The problem lies not in wealth but in the greed for gain, for many rich men have been found who gained their souls by not being entangled in wealth.
* Abraham was rich, and he is the first of those who sit at table in the Kingdom.
* Nor did Joseph incline when he found riches, and riches did not hinder him from the love of God...
It was easy for Joseph to walk the lofty, perfect way when he was rich.
* Riches are a good creation, which the fool defiles.
* It is hard for the rich man to enter into life because of his riches, since he loves them and cares nothing for the Kingdom.
St. Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: Fifth: Riches are passing; they leave us or we leave them:

paragraphs.text: By the very effort the rich man spends to grow richer he is exposed to losing everything he owns through a losing venture... How many rich men have lost all they owned in moments when the financial markets are struck by a sudden worldwide slump?! And how many global companies have been shattered and gone bankrupt because some company declared bankruptcy?!

However great the rich man's care for his wealth, suddenly he finds it has slipped from his hands like a bird, and as the wise man says: "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven" (Prov 23:4-5).
The rich man may spend all his effort to leave his son a huge inheritance, and behold he leaves him a fortune burdened with debts:
"But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand" [14].

entries.section: Fifth: Riches are passing; they leave us or we leave them:

paragraphs.text: If he does not lose his wealth but leaves a great inheritance to his son, he himself will leave it: "As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand" [15].
* From this world which you have loved you will carry nothing with you, except the vice which you have loved.

entries.section: Fifth: Riches are passing; they leave us or we leave them:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Finally wise Solomon presents a bitter picture of some greedy rich men who love money, for though they own much they eat all the days of their life in darkness in order to save the consumption of fuel! "All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he hath much sorrow and wrath" [17].

entries.section: 3. Joy and thanksgiving for God's gifts:

paragraphs.text: 18 Behold that which I have seen: it is good and comely for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy the good of all his labour that he taketh under the sun all the days of his life, which God giveth him: for it is his portion. 19 Every man also to whom God hath given riches and wealth, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labour; this is the gift of God. 20 For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth him in the joy of his heart.

If the lover of riches and hoarding lives as in darkness, fearing lest he consume much fuel... lives in sorrow and wrath, since he does not feel God's care for him and His concern for him, and whatever he receives he murmurs, then the true believer, on the contrary, lives his daily life using everything in his hands with joy, giving thanks to God for His gifts.
The writer offered the same counsel at the end of the second chapter, after affirming from his personal experience that sensual pleasures are unable to satisfy his heart (Eccl 2:24-26).
His counsel is summed up in the following:
a. That man eat and drink and do his work as divine gifts [18].

entries.section: 3. Joy and thanksgiving for God's gifts:

paragraphs.text: b. That he count riches and wealth also as divine gifts [19].
c. That he live his daily life with joy in the Lord [19], for "God answereth him in the joy of his heart" [20], or as some translate it: "because God gives him the desire of his heart as joy."

* It is the gift of God that man reap the fruit of his labor with joy... Such a man is not troubled, nor is he enslaved all his life to evil thoughts, but measures his life by good works, for his heart is good in everything, and exults with joy in the gift of God.

entries.section: 3. Joy and thanksgiving for God's gifts:

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker "Because God answereth him in the joy of his heart" [20], meaning that God looks upon the believing man as His beloved child, whom He occupies with heavenly wisdom, the earnest of eternal glory and the knowledge of some mysteries, like one who wishes to gladden his heart. The Evangelist says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Lk 10:21). This is God's gift to us, His children, of which the wise of this age are deprived. This gift gladdens our heart more than all the riches and wealth of the world!

1 There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men: 2 A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

The wise man shows here how much evil befalls a man if he misuses God's gifts of money and wealth. He begins his discourse by saying: "There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men" [1]. Perhaps Solomon, as a famous king to whom many came to hear his wisdom, saw an evil spreading among his people and among the strangers coming from the ends of the world; he saw it as a disease or plague that had settled in the hearts of many, the sickness of stinginess, which he calls "an evil disease" [2].

He saw a man "to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it" [1-2].

First: The writer affirms that the money and honor in this rich man's hands is God's gift, whether the man received it by the inheritance of his parents or gained it by his striving and toil... and it behooved him to thank God and praise Him, asking of Him wisdom and divine counsel that he might order his life well.

Second: This rich man has no excuse, for divine providence lavished blessings on him and he no longer lacked anything his heart desired, and as the Psalmist says: "Thou fillest their belly with thy hid treasure... As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness" (Ps 17:14-15). God in His love often gives the wicked the desire of their heart: temporal goods, and draws the heart of the believer to Himself to bear His likeness and image!

Third: This rich man did not enjoy what he received, leaving what he had to a stranger; perhaps he means that some stranger seizes his possessions, from which he deprives himself and his children of enjoyment, or that he dies without enjoying his wealth and has no son (or daughter) to inherit it, but a stranger takes possession of what he gathered... all that he gathered a stranger enjoyed!

Ephraim mixed with the pagan peoples and his life was corrupted, so it was said: "Strangers have devoured his wealth" (Hos 7:9), and the wise man speaks to the man who falls with a foreign (pagan) woman whose lips drop honey: "[Lest] thy labours be in the house of a stranger" (Prov 5:10). So sin in all its forms, especially greed and adultery, or the love of money and bodily pleasures, drives man into captivity, and the enemy of good robs him of all the divine gifts he carries; he loses his wealth, even his humanity, and is stripped of all reason and wisdom!

Sin is exceedingly sinful: its mouth drips honey and its words are smoother than oil, but like a two-edged sword it cuts into the depths to rob man even of himself! And the enemy of good takes possession of all his wealth!

entries.section: 2. Wealth spoiled by the sense of want:

paragraphs.text: 3 If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he. 4 For he cometh in with vanity, and departeth in darkness, and his name shall be covered with darkness. 5 Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing: this hath more rest than the other. 6 Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?

He gives another example, opposite to the first: a man who begets a hundred, or as the Psalmist says of some of the wicked, "They are full of children" (Ps 17:14), and lives a long time, and because of his greed feels want and dissatisfaction, since his soul remains in a state of emptiness; even if he thinks that he will have "no burial" [3], that is, that he will never die, the untimely birth is better than he, for he will not enjoy the sweetness of life but lives as in darkness because of his intense sense of need to hoard. He is like a tree that bears very many fruits, but does not offer its fruit to be eaten and keeps it on itself until it spoils and falls to the ground and gathers insects.

Perhaps he meant by "and also that he have no burial" that at his death he is "buried with the burial of an ass" (Jer 22:19); for although he has a hundred sons and lived many years gathering money, his children, because he deprived them of enjoying the goods all this time, do not care for his honor, nor do they concern themselves with his burial, but with searching for the wealth he left them and dividing it... I remember a family whose members quarreled over the inheritance among themselves while the body was still lying in a closed room, not yet buried! They were fighting instead of weeping for their father!

The wise man says of him: "An untimely birth is better than he" [3]. He concedes that the state of the untimely birth is extremely sad, "for he cometh in with vanity" [4], for in vain did the couple rejoice at the conception and the mother endure much awaiting her newborn, and the father prepared himself in mind and means for a happy event... and their hopes were disappointed, their spirits were broken and their efforts were lost in vain. "And departeth in darkness," for scarcely anyone is aware of him; before his birth could be celebrated he is buried without honor! "And his name shall be covered with darkness": the parents had prepared a name for him, which is not realized but vanishes with him into the darkness before anyone calls him by it: "Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing" [5], that is, he did not look on the sun and enjoy the light, but went out from the darkness of the womb to the darkness of the grave, and no one knew of him, nor did he himself even recognize his parents.

entries.section: 2. Wealth spoiled by the sense of want:
