paragraphs.text: This is the picture the wise man presented of the untimely birth, and yet in comparing him with the stingy man he says: "This hath more rest than the other. Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?" [5-6]. The untimely birth, deprived of the light of life and of every memory and of all knowledge... who has no social existence, is better than a stingy man who lives thousands of years hoarding money and sees no good in his life, and also awakens no happiness or joy in the lives of others... for after the misery of all these years he meets the untimely birth in the same place, "the grave"! The stingy man by his evil will has become like the untimely birth, coming in with vanity and going into darkness... for in vain does anyone hope for good from him; the love of money deprives him of seeing the Sun of righteousness and robs him of the ability to reason and of true spiritual knowledge! How dangerous is the love of money, for it makes man's life a hell and a darkness more bitter than the darkness of the grave... and finally he leaves the world naked, receiving nothing of all that he gathered.
* A camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle, nor the rich man enter the exalted Kingdom...
* Riches and gold do not remain with the one who acquires them; why does man acquire riches and gold that are not his?!
* Look at the rich who acquired names and greatness on earth: they have fallen, and their schemes and their names have come to nothing.
* The soul is greater than possessions and places.
* O my Lord, You are the wealth, the treasury and the treasure of him who possesses You; blessed is he who possesses nothing but You!
St. Jacob of Serugh

7 All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. 8 For what hath the wise more than the fool? what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living? 9 Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this is also vanity and vexation of spirit. 10 That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it is man: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he. 11 Seeing there be many things that increase vanity, what is man the better? 12 For who knoweth what is good for man in this life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun?

After the wise man revealed the danger of greed and the love of money, he goes on, as is his custom, to affirm that the money God gave us is given that we may use it, not that it may use us and enslave us.

"All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled" [7]. The money or wealth God gave us is given that we may eat and satisfy the needs of our body, but our souls are filled neither by food nor by the love of possessions, but by God Himself! The stingy man may deprive his mouth of food in order to gather money, and so neither his body nor his soul profits by it. Perhaps he means that however much the rich man gathers, he needs only to meet the needs of his body, with no difference between cheap food and luxurious... Then let him fill his mouth and the mouths of his brethren with the wealth he has!

Let the rich man fill his mouth with food and let him know that his soul will never be satisfied however much it hoards, because he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver (Eccl 5:10)... his mouth needs food and his soul needs the love of God and of his neighbor.

Perhaps by his saying "All the labour of man is for his mouth" [7] he means that what the rich man gathers is only for the purpose of stopping his inner mouth that says, "Give, give"... but his mouth remains empty and his soul is not filled!

Finally, why does the rich man toil in vain, gathering money without satisfying his soul?! For the wise man is equal to the fool in leaving behind all that they own here, and so also the rich with the poor... only one thing remains, man's true wisdom in walking among the living (the sons of men) in a spirit of pure love.
"For what hath the wise more than the fool?
what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living?"

The wise poor man lives happy, content with the food and clothing he has (1 Tim 6:8), and carries love with him into his eternity, while he who thinks himself wise and rich loses his happiness here and his eternal glory.

The Preacher's counsel to all is to walk in a spirit of thanksgiving, counting what they have, little or much, as better than waiting in a spirit of greed for what they desire and dream of in wealth and rank:

"Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire" [9]. The man who feels satisfied, content with what he has or with what is present before him, what he sees with his eyes, is better than he whose soul roams in covetousness, desiring things he may not be able to obtain.
* Be sure that the most foolish of all is he who finds satisfaction in no desire (asking for more); but the wise man is not found a captive to those desires.

St. Gregory the Wonder-worker Man's giving free rein to his desires, including the desire to possess, is "also vanity and vexation of spirit (a distress of the wind)" [9], because whenever he obtains something the flame of desire increases all the more to ask for more, and so he enters into distress of spirit! Therefore it behooves the believer to realize that what is in his hands has already been ordered for him by God, as his heavenly Father who loves him, and that He is almighty and all-wise... He knows how to give him what suits him. And if he wished to contend with Him, could he do so, when He is stronger than he and wiser and more loving? Can he change the plan of God his Father concerning him and alter His judgments?!

The Preacher says: "That which hath been is named already" [10], that is, that the Eternal, who was, had already called him by name as man. Man is unable to resist his mighty Creator... "Neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he" [10], that is, man cannot resist a stronger man, so can he resist the Creator of mankind?!

The Preacher closes his discourse with the final conclusion that what man gathers will not increase his happiness, because he does not know what is good for him [12], especially since his life, which he spends on earth, however long it is, is like a shadow [12], and he does not know what will happen after his death with regard to his family and offspring [12].

entries.section: 1. A good name is better than luxury:

paragraphs.text: "A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth" [1].

To acquire a name, a good reputation or a good fame is better than to acquire great wealth or costly perfume. The foolish man either hoards and gathers, so that neither he nor his sons nor his relative profit by what he has, or he squanders his money in extravagant living, living a life of pleasure and recklessness. But the wise man, in moderation, knows how to use the vain world without being enslaved by the world. He uses it without giving himself free rein in the love of money or the love of pleasures; he cares about the day of his death, to leave a true witness on earth, whose fragrance is better and more lasting than much costly perfume.

If the ointment here points to temporal goods, then a good name does not mean the love of passion or the seeking of vainglory, but leaving a living witness of a godly life, as happened with the woman who poured the ointment on the head of the Lord Christ, for He said: "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her" (Mt 26:13). This is the good name we acquire when we pour out our lives, poured forth like a flask of very costly ointment.

The wise man cares about the day of death, not the day of birth, and is not occupied with his temporal affairs like one who will remain in the world forever, but lifts his mind to what is beyond death, offering his life as a poured-out flask of ointment, whose fragrance spreads on earth and in heaven.

Our thinking about the day of birth is a regression to immature childhood, and a living in the dreams of the past, while our thinking about the day of death is an advance toward a deeper fellowship with the Lord Christ, who kindles our depths toward heavenly things, so that we bear death with Him every day with joy (1 Cor 15:13).

The natural man rejoices in the day of his birth and celebrates it as an annual feast, and fears the coming of the day of his death and makes every effort to postpone it as long as he can, but the spiritual man sees in the day of his birth a divine gift, and thanks the Creator who brought him into the world that He may bring him through the day of his death to a new birth, in which he meets Him face to face. The day of our birth brought us into the sufferings which we accept with thanksgiving for the sake of the Lord, but the day of death brings us into the perfect freedom of the glory of the children of God.

2 It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart. 3 Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. 4 The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. 5 It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools. 6 For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity. 7 Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart.
"It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart" [2].

In more than one place the Preacher urges us to rejoice and to remove grief from the heart (Eccl 11:9-10), for God establishes His Kingdom, the Kingdom of joy, within us. Here he speaks of repentance and preparation for eternity. In the house of mourning we see the end of the world as we see the open heaven, and long to pass over. The aim of funeral prayers is to comfort the loved ones of the departed and to open the doors of heaven before their hearts so that their souls may rejoice. The sorrow of repentance, which gives rise to inner peace, is better than the laughter of the reckless, and the sadness of countenance in the closet, not in our meeting with others, where remorse for sins gladdens the heart and makes it better!

Our awareness of the reality of death as an inevitable matter gives us a true, realistic appreciation of our temporal life and opens before us the door of hope in heavenly things, and also supports us in our spiritual striving... where we realize the shortness of the time of our sojourn, and our obligation to walk wisely and soberly instead of in excessive luxury and folly.
* An elder said: He is a fool who has in his mind the remembrance of anything of the world except the inheritance he alone will receive, I mean the grave.
St. John Saba * "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting" [2].
In the first (house) we reap the merits of good work, and in the second, a fall into sin.
In one we hope for (eternal) recompense. In the second we actually receive the reward (luxury).
Sympathize with the sorrowing as though you too were sorrowful with them!

* If anyone wishes to rise, he must not seek the delights of the world, or pleasures, or luxuries, but everything that is full of pain and sorrow, for it is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting.
Truly Adam would not have descended from Paradise to the depths had he not been deceived by pleasure!

St. Ambrose * By the latter (going to the house of feasting) the soul is inflamed. For if we can keep pace with a life of luxury we slip into indulgence in pleasure, and if we cannot, we grieve. But in the house of mourning it is the opposite; if we cannot be luxurious we do not suffer for it, and if we can, we hold back from a life of luxury.

Monasteries are truly houses of mourning, where there are sackcloth and ashes; there is solitude, not laughter nor the pressures of temporal cares. There is fasting and sleeping on the ground; there is no rich, foul-smelling food there, no shedding of blood, nor agitation, nor disturbance, nor crowding.

St. John Chrysostom * Fix the matter of your departure in your heart, O man, by continually saying: "Behold, the messenger is coming to the doors, he who comes for me; why then am I slothful? My departure will be forever, and without return!

Spend the night in this thought, and let it gladden you all day long, so that when the time of departure draws near you receive it with welcome and joy, saying: [Come in peace, for I knew that you were coming, and I have not neglected anything that profits me on this road].

* The body cannot be persuaded to live long in a state of solitude as long as it is surrounded by the causes of worldly pleasures and ease. Nor can the mind cease from them (pleasures and ease) until the body is estranged from everything done in ease. For when the body beholds scenes of luxury and temporal things, and when every hour it sees causes of relaxation, an unruly desire for them is kindled in it.
Mar Isaac the Syrian "Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better" [3].

It behooves us, while we are still in this world and feel our weakness, to practice the sorrow of repentance daily, not the laughter of the reckless and the foolish, for the tears of repentance make our hearts better.

It is not to be understood from this that the believer lives wretched and gloomy-faced before others, but that he practices his repentance in his closet, in his private life, without crushing others with his grief!
The spiritual man grieves over his sin and does not lose his peace, and so he wins others by his cheerfulness springing from inner joy together with earnestness.
"It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools.
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.
This also is vanity" [5-6].

The man who is earnest in his life rejoices at the rebuke of a sincere wise man, and is not pleased with the song of fools, that is, their flattery of him with honeyed words, for it is like thorns under a pot, which give out sounds but burn and become ashes that we long to be rid of.

The wise man, who cares for the salvation of his soul, its edification and its constant growth, not only accepts the counsels of the wise but submits willingly to his discipline and his rebuke, for "reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23); but the foolish man does not care about his eternity, so he is pleased with a life of pleasure and luxury and responds to the laughter of fools, a sign of the emptiness of his heart. The wise man says: "The end of that mirth is heaviness" (Prov 14:13). And the Lord Christ says: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh... Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep" (Lk 6:21, 25).
"Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart" [7].

If we gladly accept the rebuke of a sincere wise man who cares for the salvation of our souls, then on our part we must not be harsh to others under the cover of "the rebuke of the wise," because much oppression can make a wise man mad, that is, drive him to deviation. Therefore the Psalmist says: "For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous; lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" (Ps 125:3).
As oppression may break the righteous, so the other extreme, "a gift destroyeth the heart" [7], perhaps here means giving lavishly without wisdom, or bribery, for it drives the soul to deviation.

* It is better to receive a rebuke from a wise man than to hear a whole chorus of the wretched in their songs, for the laughter of fools is like the crackling of many thorns burning in a blazing fire.
St. Gregory the Wonder-worker

8 Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. 9 Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools. 10 Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this.
Among the counsels the Preacher offers to support man in preparing his soul for eternity are the following:

entries.section: a. Not living on the dreams of the past:

paragraphs.text: "Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof" [8]. With the eye of faith we endure to the end and are saved. We do not stop at our striving in the past, nor despair at our weakness in the present, but we must work by the Spirit of God, confident that He will surely give us victory as long as we are in His hands, trusting in Him. The prophet Moses appeared to be a failure in his ministry even after God called him and sent him to Pharaoh... but in the end he achieved unexpected success. And St. Mark also left the ministry and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13), but he came back and preached in many lands and bore much fruit... On the contrary, the Apostle Paul declares his sorrow for those who began in the Spirit and were made perfect in the flesh.

"The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" [8]. It is as though patience of spirit, or longsuffering, is bound up with humility and is the opposite of the spirit of arrogance and pride or irritability, whether within the heart or outwardly. For by pride we lose our inner peace and our eternal inheritance.

* Patience (longsuffering) is the parent of consolation, and a special power that springs from constant breadth of heart; it is hard for a man to find that power in his afflictions unless it is given him by God. He receives this gift by his earnest, continual prayers and the shedding of tears.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * There is no healing for the pain of the proud, for the more he exalts himself in his thoughts, the more the knowledge of God departs from his soul, and he descends into the depth of darkness!
St. John Saba * Pride springs from the love of money, and from the conduct that arises from it...
What madness! Does this proud man not know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and power are nothing but a deceptive mirage?!
St. Basil the Great
"Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" [9].

It behooves us to be cautious and not hasten to anger against others, because anger rests in the bosom of fools, meaning that it is born of ignorance and folly and finds its rest in it as an infant rests in its mother's bosom.

* The deadly poison of anger must be uprooted from the depths of our souls. For as long as it remains in our hearts and blinds with its harmful darkness the eye of the spirit (the heart), we cannot obtain discernment and sound judgment. Nor can we obtain true inward vision or perfect counsel, nor be partakers of life or keep righteousness, nor even have the capacity for true spiritual light, "Mine eyes are troubled by anger" (Ps 6:7). "Nor can we become partakers of wisdom, even if there should be a common verdict that we are wise, for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" [10], nor can we obtain the immortal life... "for anger destroys even judgment" (Prov 15:1). Nor can we obtain the restraining power of righteousness even if men think us perfect and holy, "for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20)... nor can we obtain even the honor and esteem that are in the world, even if they count us nobles and men of honor, "for the wrathful man is despised" (Prov 11:25)... nor can we be free from any disturbance even if no one has caused us disturbance... for "an angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression."
St. John Cassian

entries.section: d. Not being swallowed up by the past at the expense of the present:

paragraphs.text: From the events of the past we learn God's rich grace through the ages, but we must not blame the present as though God had changed; rather we blame ourselves for our weaknesses, confident that the God who worked with us in the past is able to work also in the present.
"Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these?
for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this" [10].

Let us thank God for His dealings with us in the past, and let us ask Him to work also in the present, feeling that our present existence is a divine gift, a blessing and an opportunity to receive better blessings.

The spiritual man feels that the moment he is living now is the most enjoyable moment of his life and the happiest in the Lord, realizing that it has been granted him for his repentance and spiritual growth, not that he may be occupied with the past and grieve over it as something lost, or as a happiness that has departed from him!

11 Wisdom is good like an inheritance, yea better for them that see the sun. 12 For he that is in the shadow of wisdom is in the shadow of silver, and the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.

After presenting to us practical counsels to live by, that we may live happy in this passing life and as those being qualified for the other life... now he asks us to seek wisdom and acquire it, and perhaps he means by wisdom also the Second Hypostasis: the Word of God and His wisdom.
"Wisdom is good like an inheritance, yea better for them that see the sun" [11].

Some translate it: "Wisdom is good with an inheritance," so it is good not only for the poor, giving them contentment and thanksgiving so that they find rest, but also good for the rich, teaching them how to use their money and manage it and make with it friends who will receive them into everlasting habitations (Lk 16:9). By wisdom we profit from money and gain others by it as we gain our own souls.
By wisdom also we realize that God is our eternal inheritance, and we are His portion.

By wisdom we meet the Lord Christ, the Sun of righteousness, and the eyes of our hearts are enlightened, so that our bodies see the material sun and our hearts see the Sun of righteousness... our inner enlightenment is better than outer enlightenment!
"For he that is in the shadow of wisdom is in the shadow of silver, and the excellency of knowledge is that wisdom giveth life to them that have it" [12].

If man takes refuge in silver as a shadow that protects him from many troubles, and resorts to it to buy his food and drink and clothing and also his medicine... he truly needs wisdom as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land (Isa 32:2); it is like a wall and a hedge that protects the field of the soul from the raids of enemies. And what is greater, silver does not give life to those who have it, but may even kill them if they misuse it, while divine wisdom offers us life. Therefore "How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!" (Prov 16:16).

* For the excellence of man's life does not consist in acquiring passing wealth but in acquiring wisdom. It is the greatest of all the good things obtained from God, and when we dwell in it we do not sin.
* Wisdom helps more than a company of the strongest men of the city, and it often truly forgives those who fail in their duty.

St. Gregory the Wonder-worker * For as the Preacher says: "Wisdom is a defence (shadow) as money is a defence" [12]. It behooves us not to hasten to think that this saying contradicts the word of the Lord: "Verily I say unto you, That a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God" (Mt 19:23-24), because if it were so, the salvation of Zacchaeus the tax collector, described in the Holy Bible as a man of great wealth, would contradict the Lord's declaration!
St. Jerome

13 Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked? 14 In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him. 15 All things have I seen in the days of my vanity: there is a just man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his wickedness.

The writer summarizes his philosophy of life: since our life is in the hand of God, the Almighty, Father, wise and powerful, let us therefore thank Him in the days of joy, and seek His wisdom in the day of discipline... for in His love He gives us blessings, and we thank Him, and disciplines, and we profit by them; for our edification He allows this and that.
"I make peace, and create evil (affliction): I the LORD do all these things" (Isa 45:7).
"Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?!
In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider.
God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him" [13-14].

The Preacher asks man to consider the work of God before he objects or murmurs. Neither money nor friends nor talents can change our nature and set right its crookedness and corruption, but God alone in His wisdom, as the Savior, knows how to tame us at one time by temporal blessings and at another by disciplines... and in both cases it is He who works in us. He sets this over against that, that is, He mixes days of ease with affliction, so that it is impossible for man to discover (find) what will happen to him tomorrow, and so he is always ready, trusting in God his Savior. In other words, it is to our good to accept the wisdom of God, which is able to set right our nature, without murmuring at the events that befall us.

Finally the Preacher offers his personal experience in this matter: in the days of his vanity, that is, the days in which he turned aside from God, he did not understand why the righteous are not delivered from afflictions while God is very patient with the wicked, so that it seems there is no justice or fairness.
"All things have I seen in the days of my vanity.
There is a just man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his wickedness" [15].

The righteous man may die at an early age, perhaps because God has seen him as a ripe fruit whose time for plucking has come, which would spoil if it remained on the tree. Many are taken by the Lord early to protect them from a coming evil, for the righteous is taken away from the face of evil. And God may allow the wicked to live and grow old and become mighty in strength, giving them the opportunity to repent or to fill up the cup of their wickedness.

16 Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself? 17 Be not over much wicked, neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time? 18 It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from this withdraw not thine hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth of them all. 19 Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city. 20 For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not. 21 Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken; lest thou hear thy servant curse thee: 22 For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.

When the Preacher calls us to wisdom, he is calling us to the moderate royal road, without extremism or deviation to the right or to the left, for the moderate way is the safe way that brings us into eternity.
"Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise.
Why shouldest thou destroy thyself?
Be not over much wicked, neither be thou foolish.
Why shouldest thou die before thy time?" [16-17].
What does he mean by saying: "Be not righteous over much"? Be not excessive or extreme, but walk in righteousness with deliberation, wisdom and discernment. We mention by way of example:

a. Fasting is a godly spiritual exercise, but whoever abstains from foods as something defiled or unclean falls into heresy and error (1 Tim 4:3-4). And whoever exaggerates in his fasting and so loses his ability to work and to worship has misbehaved.

* We must place the purity of our souls in one pan of the scale and our bodily strength in the other, and weigh them by the judgment of our just conscience, so that we do not incline, deviating to one pan at the expense of the other, that is, to an unseemly strictness or an excessive relaxation.
Abba Theophas b. Reading the Holy Bible is necessary, but being absorbed in it for long periods on the nights of examinations is an escape from responsibility and not righteousness.
c. Virginity is a holy way for those who have this gift... but whoever walks this way and in extremism looks upon marriage as defiled or as something despised brings danger upon himself.
* Be not righteous over much, but rather give place to faith in your mind.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * The Apostle (Paul), at the end of his discussion of marriage and virginity, was careful to show a discernment between them without turning to the right or to the left, following the royal road, fulfilling the commandment: "Be not righteous over much."

St. Jerome Abba Theonas sees, in his Conferences with St. John Cassian, and so also St. Augustine, that the phrase "Be not righteous over much" refers to those who exaggerate the outward signs of religiosity and works of righteousness for the sake of the praise of men... such people appear as wise men while they are destroying themselves by the love of vainglory.

The enemy of good knows how to destroy souls: he ruins some by stinginess under the cover of wisdom, management and discipline, and others by squandering under the cover of generosity and simplicity, and some by exaggeration in fasting and the other kinds of worship out of a desire for vainglory; and some by constant preoccupation with service at the expense of their private relationship with God under the cover of witnessing to the Lord Christ, and others by isolating themselves in their rooms while closing their hearts to their brethren under the cover of personal worship... and so on... He knows how to urge man in one way or another to turn aside from the moderate, holy royal life in the Lord.

As for his counsel to the wicked, it is not to exploit the longsuffering of God, who sometimes allows the days of the wicked to be prolonged [15]. It does not befit them to continue in evil but to offer repentance, for in this is folly and the killing of the soul and the body also... "Neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time? [17].

He calls us to a life of wisdom and moderation without slackness in the life of virtue and striving, for by this we escape the two deviations: excessive righteousness and continuing in evil. For he says: "It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from this withdraw not thine hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth of them all" [18].
As the Preacher speaks of moderation he shows us the broad lines of this way:

a. The use of a spirit of wise meekness, not domination: for many who think themselves righteous and wise seek positions in the world or in the Church, hoping that through authority they may be able to set others right, therefore the wise man calls us not to seek authority but to walk in wise love, for "Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city" [19].
* God does not dwell in the lover of preeminence, nor do you dwell with him.

St. John Saba b. Confession of sin: The wise, moderate man does not look at himself as one without sin, judging and condemning others in a spirit of authority and rebuke, but feels their weakness because he shares the same weaknesses with them. No man, even a righteous one, is without sin as long as he is in the flesh and lives on earth. "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" [20]. The Apostle John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 Jn 1:8). So it behooves all, priests, teachers and people, to confess their need of God, the Savior of the world.

* The man who is aware of his sins is greater than he who profits the whole world, and this shows in his countenance. And he who sighs over himself for one hour is greater than he who raises the dead by his prayer while living among men.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * Who among men, even if we think him a chief of the righteous saints, can at some time, while bound with the chains of this life, reach this chief good without ceasing from holy contemplation?! Is he not drawn away, if only for a short time, from Him who alone is good by earthly thoughts...?!
Who among us, even in the moment when he lifts himself up in prayer to God and soars, never falls into distraction...?!

Therefore all the saints grieve with daily sighs over this weakness of their nature. And while they search their wandering thoughts and the hidden things of their consciences and their deep solitudes, they cry out in supplication: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2); "Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?" (Ps 20:9)... "Who can understand his errors?!" (Ps 19:12). Thus they realized that man's righteousness is sickly and imperfect and always needs the mercy of God, so that one of them, after seeing the Seraphim on high and discovering the heavenly secrets, said: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5)...

You see then how all the saints sincerely confess that all men, as they themselves, are sinners, and yet they never despair of their salvation, but seek complete cleansing by the grace and mercy of God.

* There is no one, however holy, in this life without sin. The teaching of the Savior, who gave His disciples the pattern of perfect prayer, has also told us so... when we say: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12).

Abba Theonas c. Not being occupied with the words of others against you: He who walks in the righteousness of Christ does not care about the words of others, otherwise he would deviate into practicing righteousness to excess... for he who inclines his ear to the words of men finds that even those under his authority, even those to whom he provides their needs, curse him. In other words, let us be occupied with our eternity in our worship, in our teaching of others and in our daily conduct, and not care about the praise or blame of men, not because they are wicked, but because we ourselves in our weakness sin against others, even against those who do good to us.
"Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken; lest thou hear thy servant curse thee: for oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others" [21-22].

23 All this have I proved by wisdom: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me. 24 That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out? 25 I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness: 26 And I find more bitter than death the woman, whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her. 27 Behold, this have I found, saith the preacher, counting one by one, to find out the account: 28 Which yet my soul seeketh, but I find not: one man among a thousand have I found; but a woman among all those have I not found. 29 Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.

Lest it be understood from his words, "Be not wise overmuch" [16], that we should be slack in seeking wisdom, the Preacher declares his sincere longing for wisdom and his striving to attain it, so that he may be delivered from the folly bound up with evil.
"All this have I proved by wisdom:
I said, I will be wise;
but it was far from me.
That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out?
I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness" [23-25].

He set all his resolve on attaining wisdom as a way to righteousness; with all his heart, his feelings and his senses he studied, searched, prayed and sought... Thus the heart is joined with the mind, and study with prayer..., working with his whole being and all his abilities to obtain the heavenly wisdom, which is exceedingly far off and exceedingly deep... God gives it to those who seek it.

* So also Solomon, who was wiser than all men in his days or in the days before him, to whom God gave largeness of heart and an abundance of contemplation more plentiful than the sand of the sea, yet he too, the deeper he entered into (wisdom), the more his perplexity increased, and he declared his discovery of how very far wisdom is from him.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * To what extent does man pursue wisdom? And where is its perfection reached?
Truly, the limits of this journey cannot be reached, so that even the saints are found lacking in the perfection of wisdom, for there is no end to the journey of wisdom.
Wisdom thus rises until it grants the one who follows it union with God. And this is the connection: that the insight of wisdom is without limit, and that wisdom is God Himself.

St. Isaac the Syrian As much as the wise Solomon strives in seeking the wisdom that is bound up with righteousness, he also strives to be delivered from the folly bound up with evil, especially from the attachment to wicked women with whom he commits sin... For he found in the adulterous woman the following:
a. More bitter than death [26], for she causes the destruction of the soul eternally.
b. Deceitful; he calls her "snares," for with sweet and gentle words she sets traps [26].
c. Violent; she captures a man as with bonds [26], so that man loses his inner freedom, the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

d. Not truthful and not faithful, for the Preacher says: "One man among a thousand have I found; but a woman among all those have I not found" [28]. The wise man discovered that among the crowd that accompanied him, which knew nothing but hypocrisy and flattery along with a life of amusement and luxury, he could scarcely find one man who was frank and sincere in his love among a thousand men, and among the corrupt foreign women he did not find a single one who was truthful.

* It is better to renounce that woman and flee from before her, for she is a fowler's snare, and her heart is a trap, and in her hands are bonds. But the one who is righteous before God escapes from her, while the sinner falls into her snares.

St. Cyril the Great Lest anyone think that God created man evil, or that woman is more wicked than man, the wise man completed his discourse: "Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" [29]. Man, whether man or woman, has corrupted his life by his many inventions, that is, by his evil conduct and his corrupt will.

* He says that He made man upright. Consider the force of these words, for the word man means both male and female... Let us read the beginning of the book of Genesis, and we find "Adam," that is, man, meaning both the man and the woman (for Eve was in Adam), and God created him upright and good; but when we sinned we fell into a wretched state, and left the paradise that had been made good...

St. Jerome * The virtue of man and woman is one; as soon as He created them, they were surrounded with equal honor. Hear the book of Genesis: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). Since their nature is one and they have the same actions, their rewards must also be one.
St. Basil the Great * (Speaking in the person of the martyr Julitta)

We are of the same clay as men... and like them we were created in the image of God. Yes, woman is able to work virtue as men do. So the Creator willed. And in all things we are nothing but partners with them. God did not take only from the flesh of Adam to make Eve, but she is "bone of his bones" (Gen 2:23). Therefore we owe to the eternal God honor in our steadfastness, in our strength and in our patience, in the same measure as men.

St. Basil the Great * The Holy Spirit says: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" [29]. Thus it is evident that men from the beginning discovered evil, wrestled with it and imagined it in themselves, and they deserved the penalty of death with which they had been threatened. And from that time they did not return to what they had been, but were corrupted by their inventions.

Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic * We were created good by the Good (God), for "God made man upright," but by our free will we became evil. We had the power to become evil, and we were good, and we shall have the strength to become good while we are evil.

* So, as it is written: "God hath made man upright" [29], and therefore with a good will, for if he had not had a good will he would not have been counted upright. Then the good will is of God's making, for God created him with it. But the first evil will, which preceded all the evil works of man, is rather a kind of falling away from the work of God...

St. Augustine * The wise Solomon says: "God hath made man upright," that is, to enjoy the knowledge of what is good only, "but they have sought out many imaginations," that they - as it was said - wanted to know good and evil.

Abba Chaeremon * Because we sin by our free will, the prophet says plainly in a certain place: Though I planted for you a fruitful vine... how are you turned into bitterness and become a strange vine? The plant was good, but the fruit came from the evil will. Therefore the vinedresser is not blamed, but the vine is burned with fire, because it was planted good but bore the fruits of evil by its own will.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem * We must not ascribe the deviation into the wandering of the heart to human nature or to its Creator. For the Holy Scripture rightly says: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." The difference of thoughts depends on us, for the good thought draws near to those who know it, and the prudent man finds it (Prov 19:7). So whatever is subject to our discernment and our work, we are able to attain; and if we do not reach it, this is due to our laziness and neglect, not to a fault in our nature.
Abba Serenus
"Who is as the wise man?
and who knoweth the interpretation of a thing?
a man's wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the boldness of his face shall be changed" [1].

Many are afflicted with a kind of frustration or indifference when they contemplate the vanity of the world and the injustice and oppression that prevail in it, especially on the part of those entrusted with justice, whether on the religious or the civil level. Therefore the Preacher begins to reveal the importance of wisdom in man's life, regardless of what goes on around him.

a. Wisdom makes a man advance ahead of his kinsmen and makes him more distinguished than they: "Who is as the wise man?" Heavenly wisdom, as we saw before, is without limit, far off, that is, exalted to the utmost height and exceeding deep (Eccl 7:24); it lifts man up to God to grant him a life of fellowship and union with Him. There is no learned, noble or rich man who can compare with the one who enjoys divine wisdom!

When the wise Solomon spoke in the book of Proverbs about wisdom as a living being (Prov 9:1-6), he meant by it the person of the Lord Christ, "the wisdom of the Father." The wise man is the one who receives the Lord Christ dwelling in him, or receives Him as his head, and is himself a member of the Church, the Body of Christ.

Our union with the Lord Christ gives the heart sweetness and breadth, and lifts the mind above all troubles and trivialities, so that it walks in the Spirit of Christ with balance and heavenly wisdom.

b. Wisdom makes a man useful to his brethren, devoted in his service to them, for one like him "knoweth the interpretation of a thing," that is, he perceives what lies behind events and follows the purposes of things on a higher level... His counsel to them is wise and sound. For wisdom gives him an interpretation of dealings with him as with others, so that he walks and guides others according to God's good will.

c. By wisdom man comes to know God's plan and understands why relief is permitted as well as affliction, so his face is enlightened with joy and hope under all circumstances, and he even sends forth this joyful hope into the lives of his friends, so that his image appears beautiful and radiant in their eyes. Thus wisdom makes his face shine, as happened with Moses the prophet when he came down from the mountain. It honors him and lends radiance to all his speech. It makes him worthy of the attention and reverence of others, beloved by them, and changes the hardness of his face, his speech and the sternness of his features into radiant and cheerful features.
d. Wisdom (the Lord Christ) reforms the violent nature of man, for "the boldness of his face shall be changed"... It gives him enlightenment and tenderness!

* The nearer man's heart draws to wisdom, the greater the joy it receives from God. By this a person can distinguish between spiritual wisdom and worldly wisdom. And man is assured in himself that spiritual wisdom causes a silence that settles in his depths, while worldly wisdom causes a flood of slipping into error.

When you discover spiritual wisdom, you are filled with humility, gentleness and a peace that rules over our thoughts, so your members are calm and wicked passions and gluttony do not disturb you. But if the other wisdom takes possession of you, then a haughty mind takes hold of you, together with perverse and unspeakable thoughts, a scattered mind and shameful, inflamed senses!

* How sweet is the knowledge that is acquired from real experience and diligent exercises. And how great is the power it gives to the man who finds it within himself through many experiences; the same is felt by those who are certain of it and remember how much help it has provided them, so they know the weakness of their nature and perceive the measure of the divine help granted to them, which God may withhold at the beginning while they are in the midst of trials.
* The knowledge that concerns God is the queen of all longings; there is nothing sweeter than it on all the earth for the heart that receives it.

* When does a man perceive that he has received wisdom from the Spirit? From the knowledge that teaches him the ways of humility in his hidden depths and in his senses, and reveals to him in his mind how humility is obtained.

St. Isaac the Syrian St. John Chrysostom compares the beauty that wisdom reflects on a woman's features with the care for outward adornment, saying: [If a man's wisdom makes his face to shine, how much more will a woman's virtue make her countenance shine? And if you count this a great adornment, tell me what will be the value of pearls on that (last) day?].

2 I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God. 3 Be not hasty to go out of his sight: stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him. 4 Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou? 5 Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment.

Since wisdom is a meeting with God Himself, the true "Wisdom," the face of the believer is enlightened and carries within it a surpassing sweetness with a spirit of humility... this inner humility must be translated in practice into our conduct with everyone, especially by submitting to the authorities in a spirit of obedience without murmuring. The author sees that God, the Ruler of all, has permitted the existence of those in authority, even if they are unjust, so in wisdom we submit to them in the Lord. This submission rests on two principles: our faith in God's surpassing providence for us, and our enjoyment of a quiet and peaceful life.
a. "I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God" [2].

Here is a call to submit to the laws and be committed to respecting them, but the limit of this obedience is "the oath (the vow) of the Lord," that is, without violating our obligations toward God or our covenant with Him, for it is above every obligation. As the Lord Christ says: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

In the same spirit St. Paul says: "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation" (Rom 3:1-2).

b. We must not rebel against him, resist him or refuse his service because his actions are not accepted by our reason or wrong us. In wisdom we must not hasten to leave him and go out from before him, for the sake of our peace, avoiding his anger and fury. Let us wait, for God does not leave injustice to prevail but intervenes at the proper time. The Preacher says: "Be not hasty to go out of his sight" [3]. The people were hasty when Rehoboam the son of Solomon answered them roughly and harshly, and they hastened to go from his presence, indeed they cried out at once: "To your tents, O Israel" (1 Kgs 12:16), and the kingdom was divided for long centuries!

c. We must not persist in error when we discover it: "Stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him" [3]. When we think wrongly against one who holds authority, we must turn back and not go on in the error.
d. As long as we keep the commandment and walk in a spirit of obedience and wisdom, we do not fear the power that the word of those in authority holds...
"Where the word of a king is, there is power:
and who may say unto him, What doest thou?
Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment" [4-5].

The Preacher does not deny the capacity of the one who holds authority, for he cannot bear to see anyone disobey his word, and as the wise man says: "The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion" (Prov 19:12)... There is none who says to him: What doest thou? Yet there is no danger in this, as long as our hearts are pure, keep the laws and obey them gladly, and our minds are full of wisdom, knowing how to act at the proper time.

6 Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him. 7 For he knoweth not that which shall be: for who can tell him when it shall be? 8 There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it.

As long as we keep the Lord's commandment and accept the word of rulers in the Lord, we must not fear authority, nor be troubled by what may befall us tomorrow, nor even by facing death; we fear one thing only, which is to sin, for "wickedness [shall not] deliver those that are given to it."
a. "Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him."

It befits the wise man to understand that for everything there is a suitable time with God; nothing happens by chance, but by the wisdom of God, the Ruler of all. Everything is reckoned with God, and its time is appointed by a divine plan or by divine permission, but man, in his ignorance of God's plan and judgments and his lack of full trust in His surpassing providence, falls into great evil.

Man needs the enlightenment of his inner sight by the Spirit of God, so that he does not think that a certain event befalls him without purpose... but rather leans on the breast of his Creator, thanks Him for joyful events, and benefits from His chastenings, knowing that all things work together for good to those who love Him (Rom 8:28). Joseph could not have received glory in Pharaoh's palace had he not first been trained in the school of life, understanding that his brethren had done him evil, but with divine permission, who turned their evil into good (Gen 50:20).

Our great evil comes upon us not because of the circumstances that surround us, however harsh they may seem, but because of the veil over our inner sight. The work of the Holy Spirit is to give us enlightenment, so that we perceive that we are children of God, the object of His love, who cares even for the number of the hairs of our heads, who holds our hands amid events on the narrow way of the Cross so as to bring us into the breadth and joy of the Resurrection.
b. "For he knoweth not that which shall be: for who can tell him when it shall be?

There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it" [7-8].

All of us are ignorant of the future, its events, circumstances and times, and no one can tell us what will befall us so that we may prepare for emergencies. We do not know the evil before it happens so that we may avoid it or guard against it... but we know one thing by which we face the future with all its events and surprises: "neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it" [8].
We face three things:
* An unknown future, with events that may seem sudden and unexpected.
* Inability to retain our spirits when they are demanded, that is, we cannot postpone the hour of our departure from this world, where the door of repentance is closed forever.

* We cannot be discharged from the war [8], that is, from entering the battle that is raging between God and the devil, whether we enter under God's protection or accept submission to the enemy of good.

These three things are turned to our good if we entrust ourselves to the righteousness of Christ, the Giver of peace, victory and glory; if we think that we cannot live in an evil world unless we walk with cunning, craftiness and evil as a human wisdom and an experience we acquire over time, then evil will not deliver us here on earth, nor in our meeting with the just Judge on the great day of the Lord.

9 All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: there is a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt. 10 And so I saw the wicked buried, who had come and gone from the place of the holy, and they were forgotten in the city where they had so done: this is also vanity.
Perhaps someone asks: How can I obey those in authority if they are unjust and lovers of domination? The Preacher says:
"All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: there is a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt" [9].

Truly it is hard for a man to see a person who is a tyrant, a lover of domination and of oppressing others, and it is grievous to see some leaders on the religious or worldly level, instead of establishing justice, exploiting their positions for their own glory or wealth; but let these know that by this they practice what is to their own hurt.

When we see tyrants we do not condemn them but pity them and pray for them, that God may grant them a spirit of self-giving love and humility, so that they neither cause anyone to stumble nor perish themselves.

Furthermore, it befits the unjust to understand that even if they obtain something by their injustice, whether wealth or honor, they will be buried and their memory forgotten. The Preacher says: "And so I saw the wicked buried" [10], that is, their bodies are cast into the dust and their honor with them. The Preacher continues his discourse about them, saying: "And they were gathered, those who come and go from the place of the holy and receive honor, and they were forgotten in the city. This is also vanity" (10 N IV and Vulgate). Truly, as leaders who enter the sanctuaries and go out from them in grandeur, and the place of judgment was called "holy" in the Old Testament because "the judgment is God's" (Deut 1:17), as it is said that God "judgeth among the gods" (Ps 82:1), etc... Under the cover of this grandeur they commit injustice and persist in it, but their bodies become dust and their memory is buried with them... The holy city forgets them, and they have no place in the heavenly Jerusalem, into which nothing defiled or unclean enters, nor whoever works falsehood and injustice.

In their recklessness they hasten unjust judgment, and God in His longsuffering bears with them and leaves them in their positions for a time, that perhaps they may repent; otherwise their memory is buried with their bodies, and they lose both temporal and eternal things.

entries.section: 5. Wisdom and the prosperity of the wicked:

paragraphs.text: 11 Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. 12 Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him: 13 But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong his days, which are as a shadow; because he feareth not before God. 14 There is a vanity which is done upon the earth; that there be just men, unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked; again, there be wicked men, to whom it happeneth according to the work of the righteous: I said that this also is vanity.

God is patient with the unjust, and indeed with all the wicked, and the judgment is not executed speedily... But many, instead of repenting, make light of God's longsuffering. As the Apostle Paul says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:4-6). This is what the Preacher expressed, saying:
"Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil" [11].
God delays a little in punishment, but it will surely come to pass, and sternly, especially since some misunderstand God's longsuffering and fill up the cup of their evil.
Perhaps someone asks: And what of the fault of the oppressed?
The Preacher answers: Even if evil increases, it is turned into good for those who fear the Lord.
"Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him:

entries.section: 5. Wisdom and the prosperity of the wicked:

paragraphs.text: But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong his days, which are as a shadow; because he feareth not before God" [12-13].

Some may object, saying that God's longsuffering has reached a limit beyond what we expect, and the days of the wicked man have been prolonged so that he commits evil not once or twice or ten times but a hundred times; but let these know that the people of God, or those who truly fear Him, even if oppression falls upon them hundreds of times, are a blessed people. They fear the Lord, therefore He accompanies them in the darkest circumstances; nothing can shake their happiness, nor can anything cut off their fellowship with God; even in the midst of their troubles they are filled with inner peace, because they are kept by God their Father, who rescues them from affliction and glorifies them.

The wicked, on the contrary, though they seem fresh like grass, are in their depths filled with misery; good finds no place in them, and blessedness does not know them. They may live in luxury for a period of time, but the curse, as the natural fruit of their deeds, surely comes upon them unless they repent and return to God in fear and trembling. As it is said: "Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him: for they shall eat the fruit of their doings. Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him" (Isa 3:10-11).
However long the days of the wicked man may be, they are like a shadow, ending without profit. We may think they are long, but in God's eyes they are like a swiftly passing shadow.

entries.section: 5. Wisdom and the prosperity of the wicked:

paragraphs.text: The thermometer by which the wise man recognizes the righteous and the wicked and distinguishes between them is "the fear of God," so he calls the righteous "them that fear God," and says of the wicked that they "feareth not before God." As for outward appearance, temporal blessings or death, the righteous may fall into afflictions and troubles that the wicked deserve, and the wicked may enjoy temporal blessings that the righteous deserve. This is what reveals the vanity of the world [14], without accusing God of injustice, for He waits to reward all and repay them at the proper time.

entries.section: 6. Reflection on God's work and gifts:

paragraphs.text: 15 Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry: for that shall abide with him of his labour the days of his life, which God giveth him under the sun. 16 When I applied mine heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth: (for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes:) 17 Then I beheld all the work of God, that a man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun: because though a man labour to seek it out, yet he shall not find it; yea further; though a wise man think to know it, yet shall he not be able to find it.

The injustice that befalls the world reveals the vanity of the world, but it does not make the believer lose his inner joy; rather he gives thanks to God under all circumstances, counting his eating, drinking and labor as God's temporary gift [15]. This is what the wise man repeats in more than one place (Eccl 2:24; 5:18).

The wise man stresses the believer's enjoyment of joy as the food of the soul: "I commended mirth," counting it a divine gift... The secret of his joy is his contemplation of God's work on earth and his contact with His wonders, which took sleep from his eyes, so that he remains rejoicing day and night in God who works in his life and in the lives of others... even though his personal wisdom prevents him from knowing all the secrets of God's dealings with him and His surpassing care for His children.

entries.section: 6. Reflection on God's work and gifts:

paragraphs.text: He says: "When I applied mine heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth: for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes" [16].

entries.section: 6. Reflection on God's work and gifts:

paragraphs.text: The wise man himself meant that in his inquiry into God's providence he did not see sleep... but, as he says: "Though a wise man think to know it, yet shall he not be able to find it" [17]... His wisdom is unable to find or discover God's plan and His wonderful purposes, which surpass the mind!

Let us walk in divine wisdom, so that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened and His grace may shine on our features, and with joy let us walk in a spirit of obedience and submission, and if injustice is found, let us believe in God our Father, who redeems our life from the pit and turns troubles to our good. He is patient with the wicked that perhaps they may return to Him, otherwise their lives become like a worthless shadow... How wonderful is Your work, O Lord! Grant me understanding and enlightenment, that I may perceive by Your Holy Spirit Your plan for me!

entries.section: 1. Man's inability to know God's purposes:

paragraphs.text: 1 For all this I considered in my heart even to declare all this, that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God: no man knoweth either love or hatred by all that is before them. 2 All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath. 3 This is an evil among all things that are done under the sun, that there is one event unto all: yea, also the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
"For all this I considered in my heart even to declare all this, that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God:
no man knoweth either love or hatred by all that is before them" [1].

* The meaning is that I have given my heart to contemplation, longing to know whom the Lord loves and whom He hates. And I found in truth that the works of the righteous are in the hand of God, but as to whether they are loved or hated by God, they waver, not being certain of it.
St. Jerome The obscurity of the text raises many questions, among them: how is it that the believer does not know whether he is loved by God or not? And does God hate anyone?

What the Preacher affirms is that all the righteous and the wise, with all their works, are in the hand of God, whether their days are full of joy or of sorrow and troubles... It is not fitting for the true believer to doubt God's providence for him and His care for all his affairs, small and great. But man in his weakness stands wavering, asking: Does God love him or hate him? In the bitterness of affliction thoughts pass through him to crush him: that God is taking vengeance on him, or hates him, or does not feel his weaknesses. For this he often asks: Why does God permit me harsh trials that almost crush my spirit and make me lose my faith?

entries.section: 1. Man's inability to know God's purposes:

paragraphs.text: Perhaps what causes some to stumble is that they see no difference between what befalls the righteous and the wicked, the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean, him that sacrificeth (offers a sacrifice to God) and him that sacrificeth not, him that sweareth (falsely) and him that feareth an oath... so that in their astonishment and confusion they become like those in a state of madness [2-3], not knowing the interpretation of the events that befall them and those around them.

In truth, even though the life of the righteous and all their works are in the hand of God, it is difficult for the natural man to perceive this because of the similarity of outward circumstances for the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish, and it is dangerous to measure God's love for us by outward circumstances.

Would that we were not preoccupied with outward events but looked into our depths to see the hand of God at work establishing His Kingdom in us, and saw Him setting up the icon of His heavens in us, so that we rejoice and exult, and He also rejoices in us when He sees us as His little children who perceive His wisdom and enjoy it, as the Evangelist says: "Jesus rejoiced in spirit and said: I thank You, O Father... because You have hid these things from the wise and revealed them unto babes" (Mt 11:25). He rejoices in the little children who are prepared by His heavenly revelation and His wisdom for the eternal wedding feast.

* Alas for the frailty and passing of human nature! Yet our faith in Christ lifts us to heaven and promises us the eternity of our souls. As for material conditions in life, they are the same for us and for the beasts also.
St. Jerome

entries.section: 2. God gives us opportunities for repentance:

paragraphs.text: 4 For to him that is joined to all the living there is hope: for a living dog is better than a dead lion. 5 For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. 6 Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun.

What grieves the heart of the Preacher is that God gives man opportunities for repentance in this life, so that he may return to himself and contemplate God's dealings with him instead of being confused by the outward events that crush his spirit, but instead of benefiting from them his heart is filled with evil and folly until death overtakes him suddenly.
The wise Solomon compares the living and the dead, making clear the following:

entries.section: a. The living man, for whose repentance we hope:

paragraphs.text: As for the dead man, he has lost the opportunity of repentance: "For to him that is joined to all the living there is hope: for a living dog is better than a dead lion" [4]. If a man reaches such uncleanness that he is called a "dog" - for dogs in the Old Testament were among the unclean animals much hated by them, so that they called the pagan Gentiles by this name - he is better than a dead lion.

A man may look upon himself as a dog because of his many weaknesses and falls, but in a spirit of humility he gains new life and becomes better than the one who prides himself on his own righteousness, counting himself a lion, for by pride he has become dead!

* Many of the righteous have fallen from their righteousness, and many sinners have taken their place; therefore it is not fitting for the righteous man to exalt himself, for he is still in the flesh, nor is it fitting for the sinner to despair, for God is near to him if he seeks Him, and is ready to receive him if he changes his way of life and turns to (the Lord).

St. Isaac the Syrian A man of few gifts, if he thinks in himself that he has no part in life and no authority or power, like a despised dog (in the eyes of the Jews), when he is united with the living Christ, risen from the dead, becomes better than one who has many gifts and abilities, and temporal glory and majesty like the lion, but who, by withdrawing from his Savior, loses his life and is counted dead! Our life is in Christ, and our resurrection through Him is better than every ability or greatness!

entries.section: b. The living man who is sincere with himself prepares for the day of his departure:

paragraphs.text: "For the living know that they shall die:

entries.section: b. The living man who is sincere with himself prepares for the day of his departure:

paragraphs.text: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten" [5].

entries.section: b. The living man who is sincere with himself prepares for the day of his departure:

paragraphs.text: Every human being is aware of this truth, that he will surely die... But the living man who is careful for the salvation of his soul and concerned for his eternity enjoys an effective knowledge that drives him to prepare for that day, whereas he who has died without repentance no longer has knowledge, because he has really died and has no return to life here to strive and receive a reward, but he and all his works have come into the realm of oblivion. Where has his love of the world gone? Where is his hatred of others and his envy of them? All this has perished with him, and neither he nor his works have a portion in eternal life [6].

entries.section: 3. Let us work for the eternal wedding feast:

paragraphs.text: 7 Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works. 8 Let thy garments be always white; and let thy head lack no ointment. 9 Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun. 10 Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.

If death closes the door of repentance completely, and man loses all that he gathered in this life as long as he is outside the circle of the Lord, then it befits us to work while we are alive; to work in the spirit of divine wisdom to prepare for the eternal wedding feast. The Preacher offered the following counsels:

entries.section: a. Let us live our lives with joy, with a good heart:

paragraphs.text: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works" [7].

The Preacher often repeats our duty to use God's gifts, even the temporal ones, with spiritual joy and a spirit of thanksgiving to God... Let us eat, drink and work in a spirit of moderation. "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Cor 10:31).
The life of joy here amid sufferings prepares the soul for eternal joy, where there is no affliction or pain but constant joy and a wedding feast that never ends.

entries.section: b. Let us enjoy the heavenly feast:

paragraphs.text: The Bridegroom offers us His Body as bread that gladdens the soul and His Blood as wine that cheers it... and through this wondrous sacrament He abides in us and we in Him, so we are counted the object of the Father's pleasure, and He is pleased with all our works.
* Solomon, referring to that grace, says in the book of Ecclesiastes: "Come, eat thy bread with joy" - of course the spiritual bread - "Come" is a joyful call to salvation and blessing.
"And drink thy wine with a merry heart (with a joyful soul)," that is, the spiritual wine.
"And pour oil upon thy head." Here you see how he points to the mystical anointing.

"Let thy garments be always white; for God now accepteth thy works" [7-8]. Now that you have put off your old garments and put on spiritual white, you must keep your garments always white. I do not mean that you must always wear white clothes, but that you must be clothed in true purity and spiritual radiance, so that you may say with the blessed Isaiah: "My soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of gladness" (Isa 61:10).

St. Cyril of Jerusalem And it is wonderful that when the Lord Christ offers us His Body and Blood, given for us as a joyful food that prepares us for the eternal wedding feast through our union with Him, He calls them "thy bread" and "thy wine." He has become our possession, so they are counted our bread and our wine, indeed in an intimate personal relationship, as being my bread and my wine!

Whenever we enjoy the service of the Eucharist (the Divine Liturgy), we realize that we are receiving the pledge of the eternal wedding feast and the heavenly banquet; we feel an inner rejoicing of heart, and God's longing and His pleasure in us in Christ Jesus, the Bridegroom of our souls. We put on our Christ as a robe of righteousness that removes our nakedness and takes away our shortcomings, and we enjoy His splendor upon us.
Let us take care to put on the wedding garment here, so that we may not be deprived of the wedding feast and union with our Bridegroom.
* I have often praised the virgins, widows and married women who have kept their garments always white, who follow the Lamb whithersoever He goeth.

* We are told that the Bridegroom feeds among the lilies, that is, among those who have not defiled their garments, for they have remained virgins (spiritually), and have listened to the Preacher's saying: "Let thy garments be always white."

* He who does not have the wedding garment and has not kept that commandment, "Let thy garments be always white," is bound hand and foot, so he does not know how to recline at the table or sit on a throne or stand at the right hand of God, but is cast into Gehenna, where there is wailing and gnashing of teeth.
St. Jerome

entries.section: c. Family warmth, a pledge of heavenly love:

paragraphs.text: The spiritual man sees in his holy family life a living image of the heavenly family; the family love he practices extends into heaven as an eternal love...

entries.section: c. Family warmth, a pledge of heavenly love:

paragraphs.text: "Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun" [9].

It befits the married believer to practice his married life with sincere love, counting his marriage a divine gift... Truly the life he lives is short and passing, so that those who marry are as though they did not marry, but it is God's gift that man lives, that he may hear the voice that says: "Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things" (Mt 25:21, 23; Lk 19:17)... His short life is his portion from the Lord, bearing many troubles because it is a life "under the sun," but his faithfulness in it lifts him up to a life of everlasting wedding feast above the sun, in which he finds no weariness.
"Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest" [10].

As long as we have not yet departed to the tomb (perhaps by the grave he meant the tomb), it befits us to strive earnestly with all our strength so that we may enjoy spiritual knowledge and heavenly wisdom, and be made worthy of the heavenly wedding feast. Let us bear the Cross here, and we shall enjoy the everlasting feast of the Resurrection.
* The way of the Lord is a daily cross; no one ascends to heaven in ease (comfort), for we know where the way of comfort leads and where it ends.

St. Isaac the Syrian * Grace is always ready! It seeks those who receive it with all welcome. So when our Lord sees a soul that is watchful and aflame with love, He pours out His riches upon it in abundance and plenty above all its requests.
* Be sure that it is impossible for a man to put forth all his effort to be saved, and do all that is in his power, and God leave him.
St. John Chrysostom * If you grieve (in striving) in seeking Him, you will rejoice in His presence!
* He who is diligent and seeks finds, and he who is slothful remains in blindness, in the outer darkness with the people of the left hand like himself.
* Work diligently, and you will see the tree of life blossom in the midst of your paradise.
St. John Saba

entries.section: 4. Work is of no avail without grace:
