paragraphs.text: 11 I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
When the Preacher calls us to daily striving to prepare for the eternal wedding feast, he affirms that our striving is of no avail unless God works in us.

"I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all" [11].

So if a man attains success in his running, he relies on God and not on the lightness of his body; in his struggle against sin he depends on the grace of God and not on his own strength and righteousness; in his success in practical life he does not obtain his bread by human wisdom but by God's providence for him; the wealth he enjoys does not rest on his own understanding but on the blessing of the Lord; and the favour he has in the eyes of men is not due to his knowledge and learning... For an entire army fled before Jonathan and his armourbearer (1 Sam 14:12-15). As it is said: "One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you" (Josh 23:10). God is the secret of our success, our victory, our satisfaction, our wealth and our wisdom.

* However much you hasten in running, and however much you multiply your struggles, you need One to give you the crown. "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain." And he says that I know that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor victory to the fighters, nor the harbors of safety to the valiant soldiers, but victory belongs to God, and to Him belongs the reaching of the safety of righteousness.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * The man who doubts that God helps him in good work is like one who flees from his shadow, and he suffers in time of luxury and wealth and is tempted in time of ease, and affliction comes upon him! But he who puts his trust in God is steadfast of heart, and proclaims his worthiness to all men, and his praise comes before the face of his enemies.
* No man can obtain spiritual knowledge unless he changes and becomes like a little child.
St. Isaac the Syrian * We cannot run in the way of God unless we are carried on the wings of the Spirit.
* None is stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, as none is weaker than he who is deprived of it.

St. John Chrysostom When the Preacher calls us to striving that rests on God's free grace, he affirms to us the necessity of our readiness at any moment, because we do not know the times and seasons, for he says: "Time and chance happeneth to them all," or "the hour and events come upon them suddenly" [11].

12 For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them. 13 This wisdom have I seen also under the sun, and it seemed great unto me: 14 There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it: 15 Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man. 16 Then said I, Wisdom is better than strength: nevertheless the poor man's wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard. 17 The words of wise men are heard in quiet more than the cry of him that ruleth among fools. 18 Wisdom is better than weapons of war: but one sinner destroyeth much good.

Man does not know what time may bring upon him by surprise, for he is like the fish that may rejoice in food offered to it and finds itself in a net, and like the bird that finds itself caught in a snare [12]. We do not know what troubles await us and what the day offers us... Our souls may be required, we may bear some trial, and we may enjoy relief!

Our weapon before time, with all the joys and troubles it carries, is true wisdom: "This wisdom have I seen also under the sun, and it seemed great unto me" [13]. He means here the wisdom that enables a man who loves his country and mankind - at the expense of his personal comfort - to deliver his city from imminent danger, from an army besieging it... and in this he does not ask for a word of praise!
"There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it:
Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city;
yet no man remembered that same poor man" [14-15].

What is this city but man, who carries powers and potentials of soul and body, of emotions, feelings, mind, gifts, and so on... He is like a little city with few men within it, and the devil is like a great king besieging it, for with all the devil's mighty capacities he covets man, wanting to snatch him from the hand of God to join him to his kingdom, and to subject him for his own account, insulting him and tormenting him as one taking vengeance on him. He builds great bulwarks against him to ruin him, since he wishes to establish his kingdom in him and make of him a battlefield against good... Before this might man fears and trembles, at one time for the sake of material gain, at another for pride, at a third as a kind of surrender, and so on... But the poor wise man who delivers the city by his wisdom is the Lord Christ, who emptied Himself and took our nature, and offered us His Cross to declare that His weakness is stronger than strength, and His poverty richer than all riches! Yet no one remembers this man, for all forsook Him at the Cross... He became, in the shame of the Cross, outside the camp! He came unto His own, and His own received Him not.

So let us possess our Christ, the true "Wisdom," for it is said: "Then said I, Wisdom is better than strength." The devil is strong, and sin is exceedingly sinful, but the wisdom of Christ overcomes them. Yet we must distinguish between constructive heavenly wisdom and entanglement in the philosophies of the world if they conflict with the life of faith. St. Basil the Great says:

[I have wasted much time in vanity, and spent most of my youth in the empty labor to which I devoted myself, learning the teaching of a wisdom that God has made foolish (1 Cor 1:20), until the day came when, as though I had awakened from a deep sleep, I looked upon the brilliant light of the truth in the Gospel and saw the vanity of the wisdom of the princes of this world, that come to nought (1 Cor 2:6). Then I wept over my wretched life].

If the devil, with his works of evil and with death, is like the cry of a strong man who ruleth among fools, yet the quiet of the wise Christ is greater... He came not crying out, and no one heard His voice, and behold He shatters the violent cries of the enemy, giving us His own Spirit that we may overcome by quiet wisdom.
"The words of wise men are heard in quiet more than the cry of him that ruleth among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war" [17-18].

Let us be united with the Lord Christ, the Giver of victory against the devil who rules, and let us also lessen friendship with the wicked lest they corrupt our fellowship with the Lord Christ. "But one sinner destroyeth much good" [18].

entries.section: 1. A warning against a little folly:

paragraphs.text: 1 Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour and ferment: a little folly is weightier than wisdom and honour. 2 A wise man's heart is at his right hand; but a fool's heart at his left. 3 Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool.
"Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour and ferment:
a little folly is weightier than wisdom and honour" [1].

The perfumer spends every effort to offer a precious perfume, but if a small fly falls into it, it stinks and ferments and spoils all the labor and the materials he used. So every laxity toward folly, however trivial it may seem, destroys what the spiritual man has gained of wisdom and spiritual honor through hard striving.

* When the wretched man is troubled by flies he himself becomes a fly, belonging to Satan. It is said that "Beelzebub" really means "prince of flies" or "king of flies" [whoever worships him becomes a fly].
St. Augustine * Beware of trifling matters lest you fall into their great ones. Do not be slack in your work, lest you be put to shame when you are found among your companions.

St. Isaac the Syrian Life in Christ Jesus our Lord, or the wise spiritual life, is a perfume that spreads to fill the whole house with the sweet fragrance of Christ, yet making light of what we think to be trivial small matters ruins our life and makes us like flies. Therefore the Preacher reveals to us a spiritual line of defense, saying:

entries.section: 1. A warning against a little folly:

paragraphs.text: "A wise man's heart is at his right hand; but a fool's heart at his left" [2].

The first sets his heart on goodness, or on the Kingdom of God, to enjoy the right hand of God, while the second has all his energies absorbed in evil, in the kingdom of darkness, so his lot is with those of the left. In other words, the right hand signifies concern for heavenly things, while the left signifies entanglement in temporal things.

entries.section: 1. A warning against a little folly:

paragraphs.text: "Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool" [3].

The fool practices his folly all along the way, at every opportunity, wherever he is found, without restraint... and without occasion "he saith to every one that he is a fool," declaring his folly without shame or modesty... as though folly had become his nature, which he cannot hide.

The fool, without heavenly wisdom, does not grow wiser with the days, but with time loses even natural understanding, "for unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath" (Mt 25:29).

entries.section: 2. A warning against confronting injustice with violence:

paragraphs.text: 4 If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences. 5 There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceedeth from the ruler: 6 Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in low place. 7 I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth. 8 He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him. 9 Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby. 10 If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to prosper.

Some see that the wise Solomon here guides the people to walk in a spirit of submission to those in authority, perhaps because some of the rich had rebelled against him on account of the increase of taxes owing to his many projects, and had threatened disobedience and revolt.

entries.section: a. Quarreling with rulers is not fitting:

paragraphs.text: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences" [4].

If the governor or the king is angry with you because of a slander that reached him, do not leave your place, that is, do not abandon your national role. Be calm. Do not rebel against him but wait quietly, practicing positive work, and you will win him for yourself and for others!

entries.section: a. Quarreling with rulers is not fitting:

paragraphs.text: The wise Solomon regards it as a grievous thing that happens under the sun that the base occupy some positions of leadership while the wise, the understanding and the faithful are left behind. Some fools occupy the highest posts and lofty offices while the wise are left in lowly positions. He saw servants upon horses and princes walking as servants upon the earth [7], meaning that those without knowledge or experience have occupied leading positions, walking in displays of grandeur and pomp, while those of rare competence are despised.

The wise Solomon saw all this "under the sun" [5], where injustice and disorder often rule human life through the ages, but in the other life, where there is no need of the sun (Rev 21:23), justice, love and holiness reign!

St. Jerome sees that the spirit of the ruler here [4] refers to the devil, who does not cease attacking the children of God, those who by the quiet Spirit of the Lord Christ shatter his plans and snares, and close the doors of their hearts in his face, shattering his domination and violence.

* Why do you shut the doors of your heart in the face of the Bridegroom? Open them to Christ and close them before Satan, as in the saying: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place."
St. Jerome He also speaks of the spirit of the ruler as a symbol of sin, which must be met with the quiet Spirit of Christ.

* Let us return first to the text quoted: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place." This phrase is followed by the words: "for yielding pacifieth great offences," that is, if the serpent finds its way into your thoughts you must keep your heart with all diligence, singing with David: "Cleanse thou me from secret faults. Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins," and so you do not slip into the great transgression, that is, falling into sin in deed.
St. Jerome

The wise Solomon offers a common counsel to the unjust among those in authority and to the people, asking the unjust to cease from his injustice because what they practice against others comes upon him, and calming the fears of the oppressed, who must keep within their limits, not out of surrender and weakness, but out of faith in the justice of God, who permits him who fills a cup for his brethren to drink from it himself: "He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him" [8].

Haman prepared a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it (Esth 7:10), and the inventor of the Guillotine, which bore his name, was executed by it... But what is greater, the Cross by which the devil thought to destroy the Lord Christ and blot out His name, behold it destroys the powers of Satan and scatters his authority over the believers.

Whoever breaks down a hedge behind which a believer shelters is bitten by a serpent hiding in it, for serpents often take shelter in old ruins or an old crevice. In other words, whoever is intent on tearing down the walls of others instead of working constructively in his own life or the life of others, the serpent of envy and hatred bites him, and he dies and perishes eternally.
* He who scatters the safety of others falls by the bite of the serpent.
St. Gregory the Wonderworker The Preacher continues his discourse, saying:
"Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby.
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength" [9-10].

He who removes stones in order to bring down a building has a stone fall on his head and is hurt, and then he regrets what he did, wishing he had left the stones in the building without pulling them out. Perhaps by this he means that he who opposes those in authority with the aim of reform, by biting criticism, loses much himself while he shakes others.
Likewise, he who cleaves wood with a blunt iron tool is forced to strike with force and risks the head of the tool flying off and striking him.

In all the preceding examples the Preacher affirms that the reform of rulers is not achieved by violence and biting criticism but by a spirit of meekness and love, with reliance on the work of God and faith in His justice... This is the wisdom of which he says: "But wisdom is profitable to prosper" [10], that is, by quiet wisdom our guidance of those in authority and of our own lives succeeds. Wisdom shatters the pride of the unjust and gives those who practice it the ability to work in a spirit of sincere obedience.

entries.section: 3. A warning against the evil tongue:

paragraphs.text: 11 If the serpent bite without enchantment, there is no profit to the enchanter. 12 The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself. 13 The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness: and the end of his talk is mischievous madness. 14 A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him? 15 The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city.

Having called those in authority and those under them to a spirit of quiet wisdom that gives success to both parties, the Preacher translates this wisdom practically by warning against the evil tongue as against the bites of the deadly serpent, asking us to have the anointing of grace on our lips so that we do not speak foolishly.
"If the serpent bite without enchantment, there is no profit to the enchanter (so the one of evil tongue does no better than it)" [11].

If the rebel is like a serpent that bites, let us enchant him with meekness and wise love before he bites us, as Jacob did when he offered a gift to Esau in a spirit of humility (Gen 32:13-21), and as Abigail did with David in his rage against Nabal her husband (1 Sam 25:18-35).

entries.section: 3. A warning against the evil tongue:

paragraphs.text: The wise man meets the rage of others with a spirit of meekness and grace, but the fool's mouth drives him into folly and madness... He multiplies words without realizing the consequences [14], so he falls into weariness, that is, his strength fails, and he loses the ability to know the way by which he enters the city. In other words, violent words make man lose wisdom, even natural wisdom, as well as strength and knowledge, and he remains as one outside the city of God!

To this day some villagers are accustomed to call one who specializes in bringing serpents out of their holes; when they see a serpent enter a hole they summon him, and he sings and beats on the pipe or the drum until the serpent comes out and dances to the tones of the song, and then he pulls out its teeth... Then it is unable to bite even a small child (Ps 58:4-5). So if you enchant the violent man with all wisdom full of sweetness, in a spirit of sincere submission in the Lord, you shatter the fangs of his evil before he kills you. But if you let him bite you, enchantment does not help once his venom has spread through your body.

Abba Moses, in his conferences with St. John Cassian, sees that the enchantment here is the confession and disclosure of sins, for it shatters the power of the living devil and removes from us the deadly venom of sin. He says: [The bite of a serpent without an enchanter present is dangerous, that is, the danger is that no suggestion or thought arising from Satan be disclosed to the enchanter in confession. By the enchanter I mean the company of spiritual men who know how to treat wounds with the words of Holy Scripture, and draw the deadly venom of the viper from the heart].

* If the serpent - Satan - secretly bites a person, it afflicts that person with the venom of sin. And if the afflicted one remains silent and does not repent and does not want to confess his wound to his brother and his master, then his brother and master, who have his cure, cannot help him well, for if the patient is ashamed to confess his wound to the physician, the medicine does not heal him...
St. Jerome The wise Solomon compares the words of the wise man with the words of the fool thus:

a. The words of the wise man reveal the grace of love, calm and wisdom in his heart, while the words of the fool reveal the corruption of his heart, so they expose him to mockery and ridicule and even destruction: "The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself" [12]. The Lord Christ says: "For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37), and the Psalmist says: "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves" (Ps 64:8). And as Solomon said of Adonijah, who asked for his father's wife to be his wife: "Adonijah hath spoken this word against himself" (1 Kgs 2:32).

b. The fool begins his words by revealing the folly of his heart, which is his evil spring, and his corrupt treasure that brings forth foolishness; this spring gradually bursts forth through the fool's rashness in his words until it sends out fiery missiles and turns him into a state near to madness, so that no one can control his tongue or master his words: "The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness: and the end of his talk is mischievous madness" [13].

c. The fool repeats his idle words and thinks that by this he prevails, but in reality he loses the battle during his life and even after his death, for the traces of his evil words keep pursuing him even after death. "A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him?" [14].

entries.section: 3. A warning against the evil tongue:

paragraphs.text: d. Since the fool speaks with rage and without stopping, he not only loses the battle - that is, loses his right - but falls into weariness because of his psychological fatigue and his sense of failure and injustice: "The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them" [15].

e. The Preacher ends his discourse here by saying of the fool who is proud in his folly: "because he knoweth not how to go to the city" [15], that is, he loses the ability even to perceive how to enter the city, which is something no man is ignorant of. And Abba Abraham says in his conference with St. John Cassian: [And so, since they stray from the royal heavenly way, they are unable to reach the city toward which our gaze has been directed. The book of Ecclesiastes expressed it symbolically, saying of it that it is Jerusalem... that is, the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all (Gal 4:26).
"Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!
Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!" [16-17].

Let us beware lest our king, "our inner man," be a child, that is, immature in heavenly wisdom, and care for temporal pleasures like eating in the morning instead of earnest work, and forget that he is noble (a son of God and a temple of the Holy Spirit), and that he should use the world to work with strength and not for pleasure and drunkenness with temporal things.

What is this land but our body, which falls under woe and curse if a soul dwells in it that is neither wise nor mature, seeking a life of amusement and license, so that our body brings forth for us the thorns of sin and the thistles of defilement, and is good for nothing... It wants to eat and drink and amuse itself without order or purpose. But the same body, if it is sanctified with the soul that enjoys the honor of Christ and is counted a queen (Rev 1:6), knows how to strive, turning the body into the garden of God bearing the fruit of the Spirit.
St. Augustine sees that the first land signifies the city of the devil and the other the city of God, for he says:
[I think it more fitting for us to quote from this book what concerns the two cities, one of Satan and the other the city of Christ, and what concerns their two kings: "Satan and Christ."]

The Preacher says: "Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!" "Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness (disorder)."

He calls Satan a child because of his folly, his pride, his rashness, his lack of skill in management and the rest of the vices for which this age is known; but Christ is the son of nobles - the free - that is, the holy patriarchs (fathers), who belong to the free city, for He was born of them according to the flesh. The princes of the other cities eat in the morning, that is, before the proper time, because they do not expect the joy that comes in its true time alone, that is, in the age to come, desiring to become happy quickly through the fame of this present world, but the princes of the city of Christ wait patiently for the time of the blessing that does not pass away.
St. Augustine

"By much slothfulness the building decayeth (falls apart); and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through. A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry the living: but money answereth all things." [18-19].

Through sloth and neglect man inclines to rest, not caring even for the upkeep of his house; damage may come to the roof and woodworm eat its timbers, and man remains in his sloth until the roof falls and he finds no shelter. The roof signifies the living spiritual building, for Peter went up on the housetop to pray and saw a heavenly vision (Acts 10:9-16). Through sloth we come down from the housetop, where the heavenly vision is, to being occupied with dust.

St. Isaac the Syrian urges us to leave sloth and strive in watchfulness, saying: [The soul that practices works of vigil and excels in them has in its will the two eyes of the Cherubim, by which it sees at all times the heavenly visions and draws near to them].
Through sloth the hands lose their ability to work and hang down in slackness.

Through sloth the house droppeth through, that is, it cracks and collapses... It is a painful sight for a man to see the roof of his house collapsing and to stand with folded hands, not moving to repair it, until the whole house collapses!
In the spiritual sense, through sloth man loses the heavenly spiritual vision because the roof of his soul falls apart, and his hands are unable to do spiritual work, and his inner man collapses.

While sloth makes man lose his ability for earnest constructive work, so that he feels that everything in him has collapsed and that he is in a state of utter helplessness, behold in a life of amusement he is exceedingly active. He makes feasts for laughter and spends his life in drunkenness, saying that he has much silver by which he can obtain all he desires. In this he cannot experience the words of our teacher the Apostle Peter: "Pass the time of your sojourning here in fear: forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Pet 1:17-19).
"Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter." [20].

Every sin begins in thought, so it must be pursued at its beginning... It is not fitting for us, as those who belong to God, to curse anyone, especially those in authority... and let us realize that what we do in secret is exposed openly. Perhaps by the bird of the air he meant spies and informers! Let us be faithful in our depths so that we fear no one. As the Apostle Paul says: "Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same" (Rom 13:3).
Let our inside be like our outside, pure, insulting no one, so that we may be filled with the surpassing peace of God.

Thus, as the wise Solomon calls us to true wisdom, he warns us of the negative side of falling into what we call trivial matters or small sins, and urges us not to confront the injustice of officials with violence, trusting in God's work with us and with them and His care and concern for us; he also warned us of the evil tongue as of madness, and asked us not to live as child kings but as noble kings and wise in the Lord, and asks us not to walk in slackness and sloth, and finally not to curse anyone even in our hidden hearts.

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: 1 Cast your bread upon the waters, for you shall find it after many days. 2 Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil shall be upon the earth. 3 If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it upon the earth; and if the tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it shall be. 4 He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap. 5 As you do not know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child, even so you do not know the works of God who makes all. 6 In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether both of them will be alike good.
The wise man offers us examples to reveal the necessity of constant striving in the work of love:
a. “Cast your bread upon the waters, for you shall find it after many days” [1].

This proverb points to generosity in giving. If the waters signify the many nations (Rev 16:5), then it is fitting for a person to cast, not only good words, but his bread, that is, from his own needs, to many, without expecting a quick recompense, but rather after many days. The work may seem outwardly to be without wisdom, since it is casting bread upon the face of the waters, so that many share your needs; but it floats and returns to you at the proper time.
Perhaps the casting of bread here indicates that almsgiving, or practical love, is like a ship sailing on the face of the waters to carry what we have safely to the heavenly harbor.

* It is believed that it is far better to be generous even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy (that is, lest we wrong a person who deserves to receive, while we think him undeserving). It seems that this is our duty, to cast our bread upon the face of the waters, for it will not be swept far away or lost before the eyes of the just Examiner, but will reach Him, and He will gather it for us as a portion that we shall receive in due time, even if we doubt that this will happen.

St. Gregory the Wonderworker It also points to the life of sincere repentance, in which God brings us into “rivers of waters in a straight way” (Jer 31:9). When the tears of repentance become our daily bread, our souls walk upon the face of the water in safety... and it carries us from the valley of tears to the joyful heavenly life.

* Cast your bread upon the face of the waters, and you will find the bread of heaven where the waters of grace are... for out of the belly flow rivers of living water (Jn 7:38)... and you will feed on mystical food.
Where there are the waters of tears and the rest of repentance, you feed on the living bread; for it is written: “They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them” (Jer 31:9).
Blessed are those whose tears are their bread, for they will be made worthy of joy... “Blessed are ye that weep” (Lk 6:21).

St. Ambrose This proverb also points to the life of daring in striving: a person casts his bread, which he needs, upon the face of the waters, assured that God will return it to him at the proper time, as the Apostle says: “For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love” (Heb 6:10).

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: b. “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil shall be upon the earth” [2].

Some see that this proverb points to continual giving: if you meet seven poor people, give to them generously, and if eight come to you after them, do not excuse yourself that you have already done good, but continue giving, because you do not know what will befall you... They are in need now; perhaps you will be in need tomorrow. Let us do good like God, who gives generously and does not reproach.

The number 7 points to the present life, and the number 8 points to the other life, after death. Let us strive all the days of our sojourn, that we may obtain temporal blessings and heavenly ones; or let us strive with love in what concerns temporal matters and also in what concerns spiritual matters, that is, let us give practical love by generosity in giving, by witnessing for the salvation of our brethren, and by caring for their eternity... By this you are kept from evil.

St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the necessity of being committed to seriousness in the daily work that concerns our temporal life, and of being faithful in what concerns our spiritual striving, saying:

[The prohibition of excessive care for the needs of our body does not at all negate care and work. For it remains for us “to labour for ourselves, not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life” (Jn 6:27), not only for our bodily need, but also to help our neighbor (Eph 4:28)...].

Others see that the number 7 points to the Old Testament, with its promises of temporal blessings, and the number 8 points to the New Testament, with its promises of blessings of the world to come... Let us then be faithful in carrying out the commandment of love and in striving in it, so that we may fulfill the commandment of both Testaments and enjoy the word of God, which upholds us against every evil.
* It was said in Ecclesiastes with reference to the two Testaments: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and even to eight.”

St. Augustine * It was rightly said: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and to eight also,” for those who have fed on the Law and been crowned with grace receive a portion by grace through either number.

St. Ambrose * The ark had its chambers, and the Church has many mansions (the plural of “station”), and eight souls were saved in Noah's ark; and Ecclesiastes counsels us: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and even to eight,” that is, believe in both Testaments.

St. Jerome * The reverence given to the number 7 makes us also revere the day of Pentecost (the fiftieth), because seven multiplied by seven gives the number 50 less one day, which we borrow from the age to come, that is, the eighth or the first, or rather the day that does not pass away; for the sabbath rest of our souls now ceases there, where a portion is given to seven, and even to eight.

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nazianzus c. “If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it upon the earth” [3].
The believer is like the cloud that overflows with love, like the rain that turns the wildernesses into fruitful gardens.

* Give generously; give a portion of what you have to many, even to one who does not know what the coming day holds in store for him. For the clouds do not hold back the abundance of rain within them, but pour out what is in them upon the face of the earth; and the tree does not remain in its place forever, even if people protect it, for the wind may bring it down at some time.
St. Gregory the Wonderworker d. “And if the tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it shall be” [3].

In the Bible the north wind signifies spiritual coldness, and the south wind, coming from the tropical regions, signifies spiritual warmth. The truly spiritual person is like a fruitful tree wherever he is found, whether in the south or in the north, that is, in circumstances that inflame the heart spiritually or among those who are spiritually cold; under all circumstances he does not cease striving for the edification of all who are around him. Wherever he settles, he feels that God has brought him there to offer good, regardless of the conditions and characteristics of those around him.

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: e. “He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap” [4].

The fearful person stays in his place without working; he fears the winds and so does not sow, and fears the rains and so does not reap, as though the writer urges us to work without hesitation and without fear of the existence of obstacles and difficulties.
In Egypt the month of Amshir, which is the month of winds and storms, is considered the month for planting trees (transplanting the seedling and planting it)...

Many cloak themselves with wisdom when they are afraid to practice good works and hold back from them. Therefore St. Isaac the Syrian says: [Do not let an abundance of wisdom become a stumbling block to your soul and a snare in your path, but let steadfast trust in God make for you the beginning of the way that is filled with blood (the way of spiritual struggle against sin), lest you be found continually in want and stripped of the knowledge of God, for the fearful man who watches the wind never sows].

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: f. “As you do not know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child, so we do not know the works of God who makes all” [5].

Let us practice the work of love continually without fear, trusting in God, who works in nature on our behalf and who works in our lives; for it is He who set the laws of the winds with wondrous precision, and it is He who creates the bones of a person while he is in his mother's womb. We do not know precisely the movement of the wind or how the bones are created, but we enjoy the wondrous works of God, which cannot be comprehended.

In other words, the wise man asks us to practice practical love with our brethren without human calculations, trusting in His promises to us that He repays us our love for our brethren with His surpassing love, in ways that exceed our plans and our understanding.
g. Let us strive in the way of practical love all the days of our life:

entries.section: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

paragraphs.text: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether both of them will be alike good” [7].

Sow the work of love in the time of joy (the morning) and also in the midst of sufferings (the evening), for you may win a soul by revealing your sincere love for it, either in the midst of its joy or of its troubles, or in both.

Strive in works of love in the morning of your life, that is, from your childhood, boyhood and youth, and also in the evening, which is old age... Whenever the opportunity is offered you, work, and do not slacken your hand, pleading that you are still young, lest you say in your old age that the time for work has been lost.

Let us rise early, offering the firstfruits of our time to the work of the Lord, and let us remain working until the end of our time, for if we live, we live unto the Lord, and if we die, we die unto the Lord; whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.

If our Christ, because of His love for us, was crucified, suffered and died to raise us with Him, it is fitting for us also to strive with love with Him and in Him, to be crucified with Him that we may rise with Him.

* If the Lord ascended the Cross on Friday, rested on Saturday, and rose from the dead on Sunday, so the mind, unless it ascends the Cross and tastes the vinegar and the myrrh, and then enters into rest from pains, is not worthy of the resurrection from its fall.

* As ploughed ground brings forth seed, so youth, because of the heat of its sharp movements, loves constant work, lest instead of good seed it bring forth thorns and thistles... (idleness is very bad)...

St. John Saba * We must die to sin and be crucified with Christ, placing all our love in Him. This is hard. But what is easy in the order of goodness? Victories are not gained by much sleep, nor are the crowns of triumph reaped in pleasures and the sound of trumpets... He who strives wins, and by labors we obtain glory.
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. A call to work for the young:

paragraphs.text: 7 Truly the light is sweet, and a good thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun. 8 For if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, and let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that comes is vanity. 9 Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. 10 Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for childhood and youth are vanity.

We ought not only to strive in the spirit of love, but also to start early in our striving, beginning our life with God in our youth; and the Preacher has revealed the motives for fellowship with God at an early age:

entries.section: a. “The light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to behold the sun” [7].

paragraphs.text: It is not a call to hard labor involving deprivation, but a call to enjoy the heavenly light, which gives illumination to the eyes, so that our inner man looks upon the splendor of God's glory and perceives His joyful heavens... we see Him as the Sun of Righteousness.
* The city of the person pure in soul is in his depths, and the sun that shines in it is the light of the Holy Spirit.

* Flee from the lusts of the world so that the light flowing from the Father may meet you, and commend you to His angels who serve His mysteries, that they may free you from your bonds, and you may walk following in His steps to the (bosom of) the Father.
* Faith in Christ is a life-giving and rational light.

St. Isaac the Syrian * Blessed is he who is worthy to enter there (the land of the spiritual ones), where the soul beholds the face of its Lord, tastes the sweetness of its God and rejoices, breathes in His pure fragrance, is enclosed in the depth of His greatness, is illumined by the ray of His beauty, and clings to Him, and does not want to leave from there.
This is the Rapture which our fathers call the vision of the glory of God. This is the pledge of the new world.
* You, my Lord, are the sun of the prudent, and from You they are illumined without interruption.
* Blessed is he who always gazes upon You within himself, for his heart is lit up to see hidden things.
* We cannot behold the sun without clear air and eyes free from disease; so we cannot behold the Sun of Righteousness while He is in the heaven of the heart without faith, love and patience.

St. John Saba The Lord Christ is the light of the world; He enlightens the eyes. He enlightens the right eye, so that it looks at eternal and spiritual things through Him, and He enlightens the left, so that it looks at temporal things also through Him, so that the believer sees the Lord Christ transfigured in his life and in his eternal and temporal aspirations, or in his worship and his daily work... He sees everything as sanctified in Him.
“For if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all...
Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth...” [8-9].

The living young person hates gloom, and God, in His love for man, wants for him a life of inner joy as food on which the soul feeds and its youth is renewed. It rejoices in the depths and translates its joy through practical conduct, in what the heart sees (the inner life) and what the eyes behold (the outward conduct).
* Two beautiful virtues are love and joy.
Love kills and puts to death the corrupt movements of the mind (such as anger, envy, etc.)...
And joy awakens and gives life to the luminous movements.
Body and soul both delight in the Lord through love and joy.

St. John Saba St. Anthony sees that joy is the food of the soul, on which it feeds in order to grow, and St. Basil the Great sees that gloom, or deprivation of joy, is the destruction of the inner man, for he says: [Gloom is drunkenness, for it extinguishes the light of the mind and blots out the light in it].

The wise man asks us to rejoice all the days of our life [8]... Does no sorrow then pass over us? In Christ Jesus we enjoy the joy of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), which the world cannot take away from our depths.

What increases our joy is that we remember the many days of darkness [8]; we remember how our Christ lifted us up to the light and removed from us the weight of our sins... we remember our weakness and are contrite, and we remember His work of salvation and our souls exult.
Let us also rejoice because, if we enter into sufferings, they grant us glories in the Lord, for he says: “for all these things God will bring you into judgment” [9].

entries.section: c. The Preacher affirms the link between gloom and evil:

paragraphs.text: Let us leave evil, to flee from gloom; let us be joined to the righteousness of Christ, to enjoy the joy of His Holy Spirit, for he says: “Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh” [10].

* The joy that is in God is stronger than this present time; whoever finds it not only does not care for (evil) lusts but will not even think of his own life, nor of anything else, if he has truly been counted worthy of that joy.
St. Isaac the Syrian * Put away grief from your body and gloom from your thoughts, apart from what your sin causes, for it puts you in constant grief.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 1. Remember your Creator in the days of your youth:

paragraphs.text: 1 Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, or the years draw near when you say, “I have no pleasure in them.”

If the world has become vain because of man's corruption and his life, it is fitting for man to be bound to God from his youth, so that vanities may not deceive him and he may not be confused by its cares... He has already spoken of the motives that drive the young person to enjoy fellowship with God (Eccl 11:7-10), especially the life of true joy. Perhaps a young man will say: Why do I not wait until old age? The Preacher answers him, saying:
“Before the evil days come, or the years draw near when you say, I have no pleasure in them” [1].

The evil days may come early, as when a person loses consciousness and so loses the possibility of repentance and return to God, or early death may take him suddenly; or the years of old age may come, and a person loses the sweetness of life... He calls us to return immediately to God, that we may experience the sweetness of fellowship with Him.

The Psalmist says: “O God, You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I declare Your wondrous works. Even to old age and grey hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I declare Your arm to the coming generation, Your power to everyone who is to come” (Ps 71:17-18).

entries.section: 2. The weakness and troubles of old age:

paragraphs.text: 2 Before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain. 3 In the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows are darkened. 4 And the doors are shut in the market, when the sound of the mill is low, and he rises up at the voice of the sparrow, and all the daughters of music are brought low. 5 Also they are afraid of that which is high, and fears are in the way, and the almond tree flourishes, and the grasshopper is a burden, and desire fails; because man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the market. 6 Before the silver cord is loosed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. 7 Then the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. 8 Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher: all is vanity.

The Preacher describes the dissolution of old age and its infirmities in descriptive expressions that are difficult to grasp now, because they are no longer used, but in general they reveal the distress of the wise Solomon at the days of old age. He gave this description to make clear that a person loses much of his vitality in his old age, so that even if he repents he does not have the capacity for the work of a young person, for his striving, and for his enjoyment of the sweetness of early spiritual life.

a. “The sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened” [2]. For a person in his old age almost loses his sight, so he thinks the light to be darkness, and it seems to him as if the clouds had drawn the curtain over the stars.
Perhaps what is meant here by the sun and the light... is that a person in his old age feels that he has lost the joy of life and its beauty, so the sun has become darkness to him...

If a person is struck with spiritual old age, his insight does not behold the Sun of Righteousness, the divine light does not shine upon him, he does not grasp the true concept of the Church as a moon illumined by Christ, and he does not benefit from fellowship with the saints as luminous stars.

b. “And the clouds return after the rain” [2]. The clouds here signify the multitude of trials that befall a person in his old age, of sufferings and sicknesses. They are like the cloud that pours down rain and returns again, then a third time, etc...
Whoever is struck with spiritual old age feels a dryness that causes him successive falls.

entries.section: 2. The weakness and troubles of old age:

paragraphs.text: c. “In the day when the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men bow themselves” [3]. This points to the weakness of the skeleton and the collapse of the nervous system, so the old man is not strong enough to face physical and psychological health troubles.

In spiritual old age, where a person is deprived of the leadership of the Spirit of God who renews our youth like the eagle, a person enters into despair, so that the strong among them becomes like a house without a guard or an army without strength! He collapses before trials and their storms!
d. “And the grinders cease because they are few” [3]. The teeth that chew and grind food fall out, so that he is unable even to enjoy many kinds of food.

In spiritual old age a person does not experience the words of the Psalmist: “I found Your word sweet, and I ate it,” because he has no spiritual teeth that are able to enjoy spiritual food and feed on it.
e. “And those that look out of the windows are darkened” [3]. That is, the senses of the body weaken, so the old man does not respond to what surrounds him.

In spiritual old age the inner senses lose their sanctity and grow dark, so they do not behold heavenly things, nor smell the sweet fragrance of Christ, nor know how to utter with the heavenly ones the celestial praises...

entries.section: 2. The weakness and troubles of old age:

paragraphs.text: f. “And the doors are shut in the market” [4]. Old people are unable to go out of their homes even to buy their essential staple food, as if the doors of the market had been shut in their faces.

In spiritual old age a person lies hidden in the “ego,” and so finds the gates of heaven shut before him because of the closing of his heart toward God and people. He becomes like one who buried his talent in the earth and did not trade with it.

g. “And he rises up at the voice of the sparrow” [4]. Because of their nervous fatigue and lack of movement all day long, they cannot bear the voice of a sparrow, so they rise from their sleep, a sign of their loss of inner rest in the Lord under flimsy excuses such as the chirping of a sparrow.

h. “And all the daughters of music are brought low” [4]. They do not share their joys with others because of their weariness, an indication of the deprivation of fellowship in praise and joy with the heavenly ones.

entries.section: 2. The weakness and troubles of old age:

paragraphs.text: i. “Also they are afraid of that which is high” [5]. They do not live on the upper floors lest they fall as they go up or down, an indication of spiritual complacency, and of no desire for spiritual growth and the constant lifting of the heart to eternity.
j. “And fears are in the way” [5]. They live in sluggishness; they do not want movement, an indication of no desire for spiritual striving and for enjoying new spiritual experiences.
k. “The almond tree flourishes” [5]. An indication of the white hair that fills the head so that it becomes like a blossoming almond tree. It represents the loss of the spiritual vitality of youth.

l. “And the grasshopper is a burden” [5]. They are not able to bear even the lightest kinds of food, like the grasshopper, which is a very light food, easy to digest. It signifies finding any spiritual exercise for building up the soul burdensome.
m. “And desire fails” [5]. The loss of every inner desire for gladness and joy, an indication that a person loses his spiritual joy, his inner peace, and his longing for heavenly things.

n. The old man, as he awaits death to enter his eternal home [5], is likened to: the silver cord that is loosed, that which binds the soul to the body, or the golden bowl that is broken, or a water pitcher that is shattered, or a well pulley that is smashed, that is, he turns into wreckage with no use; it is an approach to the return to dust. And in spiritual old age a person feels that his life is of no use, nearer to dust than to heaven!

9 Furthermore, because the Preacher was wise, he also taught the people knowledge; and he weighed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs. 10 The Preacher sought to find acceptable words, written uprightly, words of truth. 11 The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails fastened, masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd. 12 And furthermore, my son, be warned of these: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. 13 Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man. 14 For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil.

The Preacher did not want to draw the curtain on the painful picture of old age, but offered a remedy for overcoming the vanity of temporal life, namely, meeting with God, the Creator of the world and the preparer of eternal glory, through obedience to His commandment with a godly fear.
“Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter:
Fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man.
For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil” [13-14].

The remedy for the matter is clinging to God through godliness or the righteousness of Christ, who gives the fear mixed with love, so that we may gain our life in Him and enjoy keeping His commandment, awaiting the Day of Judgment as the beginning of a glorious eternal life in place of the vain, passing life.
As though his final commandment is: Fear God, and keep His commandments!
* The beginning of man's true life is the fear of God, but the fear of God cannot dwell in a soul that is scattered after external things.

* The fear of God is the beginning of virtue, and it is said to be the offspring of faith. It is planted in the heart when a person withdraws his thought from the distraction of the world in order to confine it in the depth of contemplation and in the things to come.

* Those who fear God, beloved, persevere with joy in keeping the commandments, even if the matter requires striving and toil, and they expose themselves to dangers for the sake of this pursuit of theirs. The Giver of life has confined the perfection of the commandments, their core, and concentrated them in two that embrace all: love of God, and a similar love, which is love of His icon.

* The commandments of God surpass all the treasures of the world. He who possesses them inwardly finds the Lord in them. And he who goes to his chamber continually while meditating on God, God takes him as His own aide; and for him who longs to fulfill the will of God, the angels of heaven become guides.

* There is no person in whom sin continues, as long as he walks in the way of the Lawgiver (God) and practices His commandments. For this reason our Lord promised in the Gospels that He abides with whoever keeps His commandments.
St. Isaac the Syrian * Acquire for yourself, O disciple, the love of carrying out the commandment, that you may be worthy to receive divine love.
* Do you desire to see the ray of the Holy Trinity in your soul? Keep the commandments of Christ.
* If a person does not see the sun, he does not enjoy its light; so if a person does not acquire the keeping of the commandments of our Lord, he does not delight in His light.

* The door of heaven and the door of the heart are one; if we guard our heart by keeping the commandments of Christ, the door of heaven is opened to us, for the One who dwells in us is the One who dwells in heaven.
St. John Saba
